name: Original Practice Test 2
source: Original LSAT-style questions written for LSAT Trainer (harder than the real test). Not LSAC material. MIT licensed.

questions.stimulus: Some geologists hold that the basalt columns at Varrow Ridge formed when a large lava lake cooled slowly in place. Admittedly, the columns' unusual height is just what one would expect from very slow cooling. But the lava-lake hypothesis must nonetheless be rejected. Columns that form in a cooling lava lake are nearly always vertical, perpendicular to the lake's cooling surface, whereas most of the Varrow columns are steeply tilted. Moreover, a lake large enough to produce columns of this height would have left a thick layer of glassy crust at its upper surface, and no trace of such a layer has been found anywhere on the ridge.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the argument?
choices: The unusual height of the Varrow columns is consistent with their having cooled very slowly.
Columns that form in a cooling lava lake are nearly always oriented vertically.
The basalt columns at Varrow Ridge did not form from a large lava lake cooling slowly in place.
No layer of glassy crust of the kind a large lava lake would leave has been found at Varrow Ridge.
The basalt columns at Varrow Ridge did not form through a process of slow cooling.
questions.explanation: The argument concedes one point and then gives two reasons for rejecting the lava-lake hypothesis; that rejection (C) is the conclusion. E is the trap: the argument concedes that the columns' height fits slow cooling and rejects only the claim that a lava lake was involved, so E overstates the conclusion. A is the concession, and B and D are premises.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The lava-lake hypothesis for the Varrow columns must be rejected.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Lava-lake columns are nearly always vertical, but most Varrow columns are steeply tilted; a lake big enough would have left a thick glassy crust, and none has been found.

breakdown.analysis: Classic concession structure: "Admittedly X. But Y." The "But" sentence is the conclusion, and everything after it is support. The concession (height fits slow cooling) is not denied, it's just outweighed. Prephrase: the columns did not form from a slowly cooling lava lake. It's like saying: "Sure, the dog was near the cake. But the dog didn't eat it: there's no frosting on him and he can't reach the counter." The conclusion is about the dog, not about whether the cake got eaten.

choices.note: This is the concession ("Admittedly..."). The author grants it and then moves on. A concession is never the main conclusion.
This is a premise. It's one of the two reasons offered for rejecting the hypothesis, not the thing being proved.
CORRECT. This is exactly the rejected hypothesis, stated as the author's claim: no slowly cooling lava lake formed these columns. Both premises point here.
Also a premise: the missing glassy crust is the second piece of evidence against the lava lake. Support, not conclusion.

Trap. It's too broad. The author rejects only the lava-lake version and actually concedes the height fits slow cooling. Rejecting "lava lake" is not rejecting "slow cooling." Watch for an answer that inflates the conclusion beyond what the author said.

questions.stimulus: Store manager: In early March, we lowered the price of our house-brand exterior paint by 15 percent. Total paint sales at our store from April through June were nearly 20 percent higher than they had been from January through March. We did not increase our advertising or change our store hours during either period, and no competing store in the area closed. Clearly, then, the price reduction is responsible for the increase in our paint sales.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the store manager's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: fails to consider that people may be more inclined to buy exterior paint in spring than in winter, whatever its price
takes for granted that the price reduction was larger than any reduction offered by competing stores
overlooks the possibility that the store's advertising was more effective in one period than in the other
draws a conclusion about hardware stores in general from evidence concerning only a single store
treats an increase in the store's paint sales as though it were an increase in the store's overall sales
questions.explanation: The manager compares winter months with spring months, and demand for exterior paint plausibly rises in spring regardless of price, so a seasonal pattern could explain the increase (A). C is the trap: the manager rules out a change in advertising, and nothing suggests the same advertising worked differently in the two periods. D fails because the conclusion is only about this store, and B and E describe errors the argument does not make.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The 15% price cut on house-brand exterior paint caused the rise in paint sales.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: April-June paint sales were about 20% higher than January-March; advertising, store hours, and local competition didn't change.

breakdown.analysis: Causal conclusion, so look for an alternate cause the manager didn't rule out. The manager carefully knocks out advertising, hours, and competitors, but ignores the obvious one: the two periods are winter and spring. People paint the outside of houses when it's warm. It's like saying "I started selling ice cream at a discount in May, and summer sales went way up, so the discount did it." Prephrase: the argument ignores seasonal demand.

choices.note: CORRECT. January-March vs. April-June is winter vs. spring, and exterior paint is a seasonal product. The increase could happen with no price cut at all. That's an alternate cause the manager never ruled out.
The argument never compares its price cut to competitors' prices, so it doesn't assume this. It's a made-up assumption.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Our sale beat everyone else's, so customers must have come to us. (Assumes our discount was the biggest.)

choices.note: Trap. It sounds like an alternate cause, but the manager says advertising didn't change, and nothing hints the same ads worked better in one period. You can't pick an answer on a bare possibility the stimulus gives you no reason to suspect, especially when A names an obvious one.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: We ran the same radio ad both months and sales rose, so the new product display did it. (Ignores that the ad may have landed better in the second month.)

choices.note: Wrong scope. The conclusion is only about this one store's sales. There's no generalization to hardware stores in general.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Our store's paint sales rose after a price cut, so price cuts raise paint sales at every hardware store.

choices.note: The manager talks about paint sales and concludes about paint sales. No switch to overall store sales happens.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Our paint sales went up 20%, so the store is doing 20% more business.

questions.stimulus:
Councilor Ames: The proposal to rezone the Delmont rail yard for apartment construction should be approved. The city's housing shortage is severe, and the yard has sat vacant for over a decade.

Councilor Perez: The city certainly needs housing, but the rail yard is the wrong site for it. Its soil is contaminated with industrial solvents, and cleaning it to residential standards would cost more than any developer will pay. Rezoning the yard for light industry, which requires far less cleanup, would actually get the land used.
questions.stem: Ames and Perez disagree over whether
choices: the city is experiencing a shortage of housing
the Delmont rail yard should be rezoned
the soil at the Delmont rail yard is contaminated with industrial solvents
the Delmont rail yard should be rezoned for apartment construction
light industry requires less cleanup of contaminated soil than residential use does
questions.explanation: Ames favors rezoning the yard for apartments, while Perez says the yard is the wrong site for housing and should be rezoned for light industry, so they disagree about D. B is the trap: both councilors favor rezoning the yard and differ only over what use it should be rezoned for. Perez agrees about the housing shortage (A), and Ames takes no position on contamination or cleanup (C, E).

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Ames: Rezone the Delmont rail yard for apartments; housing shortage is severe and the yard's been vacant 10+ years.; Perez: The city needs housing, but the yard is the wrong site; contamination cleanup costs too much; rezone it for light industry instead.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Ames says yes to apartments on the yard. Perez says no to housing there and yes to light industry. Notice what they share: both want the yard rezoned, and both agree the city needs housing. The fight is only about what it gets rezoned for. It's like two friends who both want to go out to dinner and argue only over pizza vs. sushi.

choices.note: Agreement, not disagreement. Perez says "The city certainly needs housing." Both say yes.
Trap. Both want the yard rezoned: Ames for apartments, Perez for light industry. They disagree about the use, not about whether to rezone. Two yeses aren't a disagreement.
Only Perez speaks to contamination. Ames says nothing about the soil, so we can't say he disagrees.
CORRECT. Ames: yes, rezone it for apartments. Perez: no, it's the wrong site for housing; rezone it for light industry. That's a clean yes/no split.
Only Perez makes this comparison. Ames never mentions cleanup or light industry, so he has no opinion we can pin down.

questions.stimulus: In the town of Halbrook, cases of a certain gastrointestinal illness rose sharply in the two weeks after a new municipal well began supplying water to the town's eastern district. The illness is caused by a bacterium that can survive for long periods in groundwater. Investigators have therefore concluded that water from the new well is the source of the recent increase in cases.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the investigators' argument?
choices: The new well passed every water-quality test that the state required before it was put into service.
During those two weeks, the western district, which continued to receive water only from the old reservoir, had about the same number of cases as in the preceding month.
Many residents of Halbrook's eastern district drink bottled water rather than tap water.
Outbreaks of gastrointestinal illness occur in Halbrook several times each decade.
The bacterium that causes the illness is also commonly found in surface water such as reservoirs and streams.
questions.explanation: B supplies a control group: the part of town that did not receive water from the new well saw no increase, which points to the new well as the source. E is tempting because it concerns the bacterium, but it suggests the old reservoir could harbor it too, which if anything weakens the argument. A, C, and D also weaken or are neutral.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Water from the new well is the source of the rise in illness cases.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Cases rose sharply in the two weeks after the new well started supplying the eastern district; the bacterium can survive long periods in groundwater.

breakdown.analysis: A timing correlation plus "the bacterium could live there." That's suggestive but weak: maybe cases rose everywhere for some other reason. The best strengthener is a control group. If the part of town that didn't get the new water had no spike, the well looks guilty. It's like testing whether a new shampoo gives you a rash: if your roommate who didn't switch has no rash, that points at the shampoo.

choices.note: If anything this weakens. Passing every required test makes contaminated water a bit less likely. At best it's neutral, since tests may not catch everything.

CORRECT. The western district, still on the old reservoir, saw no rise. That's the control group: same town, same time, different water, no spike. It rules out a town-wide cause and points at the new well.
Weakens. If many eastern residents don't drink tap water, fewer people were exposed to the well, which makes the well a less likely explanation for a sharp rise.
Neutral to weakening. Periodic outbreaks suggest this might just be one of the usual ones, not something caused by the new well.
Tempting because it's about the bacterium, but it cuts the wrong way: if the bacterium is common in reservoirs too, the old water supply is also a possible source. That weakens, not strengthens.

questions.stimulus: In the jurisdiction of Corland, evidence obtained through a search may be introduced at trial only if the search was conducted under a valid warrant or the defendant gave valid consent to it. A warrant is valid only if a judge found probable cause before the search was conducted, and a judge may find probable cause only on the basis of sworn testimony. Consent is valid only if it is given before the search begins. Police searched a storage unit rented by Viktor Mirov and found stolen equipment. The only testimony about the unit given to any judge before the search was unsworn.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: The stolen equipment cannot be introduced as evidence at Mirov's trial.
Mirov did not consent to the search before it began.
If Mirov consented to the search before it began, the stolen equipment will be introduced at his trial.
No warrant was issued for the search of Mirov's storage unit.
If the stolen equipment is introduced at Mirov's trial, then Mirov consented to the search before it began.
questions.explanation: With no sworn testimony, no judge could have found probable cause beforehand, so any warrant was invalid; valid consent, which must precede the search, is the only remaining route to admission, so admission requires such consent (E). A is the trap: nothing rules out Mirov's having consented before the search. C reverses the conditional, since valid consent is necessary, not sufficient. D fails because an invalid warrant may have been issued, and B is not established.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Evidence admitted → valid warrant OR valid consent; 2. Valid warrant → judge found probable cause before the search; 3. Probable cause → sworn testimony; 4. Valid consent → given before the search began; 5. Only unsworn testimony was given to a judge before the search of Mirov's unit.

breakdown.analysis: Chain it. Unsworn only → no probable cause → no valid warrant. So the warrant route is dead. Admitted → valid warrant OR valid consent; with the warrant gone, Admitted → valid consent → consent given before the search. So: if the equipment is admitted, Mirov consented before the search. Note every rule here is "only if": these are necessary conditions. Meeting them doesn't guarantee admission. It's like: you can board only if you have a ticket. Having a ticket doesn't mean you boarded.

choices.note: Trap. This only follows if Mirov didn't consent, and we're never told that. He may well have consented before the search, which would keep admission possible.
Not established. Nothing in the facts tells us whether Mirov consented. Possible, not required.
Reverses the conditional. Valid consent is necessary for admission, not sufficient. Consent opens the door; it doesn't push the evidence through it. Watch the "only if" direction.
The facts say any warrant would be invalid, not that none was issued. A judge could have issued a warrant without proper grounds.
CORRECT. Admitted → valid warrant or valid consent. No sworn testimony → no probable cause → no valid warrant. So Admitted → valid consent → consent before the search. That's exactly E.

questions.stimulus: Last year the development team at Ostrander Systems adopted mandatory code review: no change to the company's software can be merged until a second engineer has examined and approved it. Since then, the number of bugs reported by customers each month has fallen by 40 percent, even though the number of customers using the software has held steady. The team lead concludes that mandatory code review has substantially reduced the number of bugs in the company's software.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the team lead's argument?
choices: Code review is widely practiced among software firms of Ostrander's size.
The bugs that customers reported this year were, on average, more severe than those reported the year before.
Shortly before code review became mandatory, Ostrander replaced its simple bug-report e-mail address with a lengthy online form that customers must complete to report any problem.
Engineers at Ostrander report that reviewing others' code now takes up a significant portion of their workweek.
Before review became mandatory, Ostrander engineers sometimes informally asked colleagues to look over their code.
questions.explanation: The evidence is the number of bug reports, not the number of bugs; C gives a reason that reports would drop even if the software were no less buggy, so the evidence no longer tracks the conclusion. B is tempting, but the severity of the reported bugs says nothing about whether there are fewer of them. E is consistent with mandatory review making a large difference, and A and D are irrelevant.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Mandatory code review has substantially reduced the number of bugs in Ostrander's software.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Since review became mandatory, customer bug reports per month fell 40%; the number of customers held steady.

breakdown.analysis: Spot the switch: the evidence is bug reports, the conclusion is about bugs. Those aren't the same thing. Anything that makes customers report less, without fewer bugs existing, wrecks the argument. It's like saying "crime fell" because fewer people called the police, right after the police switched to a 20-minute phone menu. Prephrase: something made reporting harder or less likely.

choices.note: Irrelevant. How common code review is elsewhere says nothing about whether it cut bugs at Ostrander.
Tempting, since it changes the picture of the bugs, but severity isn't count. The conclusion is about the number of bugs, and B says nothing about whether there are fewer.
CORRECT. Right before the change, reporting went from a simple email to a lengthy form. That alone could cut reports by 40% with no drop in actual bugs. The evidence no longer tracks the conclusion.
Irrelevant. Review costing engineers time says nothing about whether it reduced bugs. A costly fix can still work.
Doesn't hurt much. Informal review happening "sometimes" before is fully consistent with mandatory review making a big difference. If anything it shows the change was real: sometimes became always.

questions.stimulus: Film critic: The director Lena Varga has repeatedly claimed that every scene in her film Tidewater was shot in the coastal village it depicts, during her production last year. But several scenes show the village harbor with a large stone breakwater in the background, and that breakwater was demolished three years before Varga began filming. So Varga's claim is false: at least some of the film was not shot in that village during last year's production.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the critic's argument depends?
choices: The breakwater visible in those scenes is not a replica or digital re-creation produced by Varga's filmmakers.
Varga has made misleading claims about the production of her earlier films.
No other village on that coast has a stone breakwater resembling the demolished one.
The scenes in which the breakwater appears are essential to the film's plot.
Most viewers of Tidewater would recognize the breakwater shown in those scenes.
questions.explanation: If the filmmakers re-created the breakwater, the scenes could have been shot in the village last year after all, and the argument collapses; so the argument must assume A. C is the trap: the conclusion holds whether the scenes were shot in another village or come from older footage, so it does not matter whether another village has a similar breakwater. B, D, and E are irrelevant.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Varga's claim is false: at least some of Tidewater wasn't shot in that village during last year's production.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Several scenes show the village harbor with a large stone breakwater; that breakwater was demolished three years before filming began.

breakdown.analysis: The critic reasons: the breakwater was gone during filming, so any scene showing it can't have been shot there then. That only works if what we see on screen is the real breakwater. If the crew built a replica or added it digitally, the scenes could have been shot in the village last year after all. Prephrase: the breakwater on screen is the real, original one. It's like proving a photo is old because it shows a building that's been torn down, which fails if the photo was photoshopped.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it and the argument collapses: if the breakwater is a replica or digital effect, the scenes could easily have been shot in the village last year.
choices.negation: The breakwater visible in those scenes is a replica or digital re-creation produced by Varga's filmmakers.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Her track record on other films has nothing to do with whether this claim is false. Negating it doesn't touch the argument.
choices.negation: Varga has not made misleading claims about the production of her earlier films.

choices.note: Trap. If another village had a similar breakwater, maybe the scenes were shot there. But that still means they weren't shot in this village, so the conclusion survives. Negating it doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: Some other village on that coast has a stone breakwater resembling the demolished one.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Whether the scenes matter to the plot has nothing to do with where they were shot. Negating it does nothing.
choices.negation: The scenes in which the breakwater appears are not essential to the film's plot.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The critic's argument rests on the facts about the breakwater, not on what viewers notice. Negating it does nothing.
choices.negation: Most viewers of Tidewater would not recognize the breakwater shown in those scenes.

questions.stimulus: Linguists studying immigrant communities in the Pell Valley have found that when immigrant children become fluent in the regional language at an early age, their families' ancestral language typically disappears from the home within two generations. Children of families who immigrated from Darnesia almost always become fluent in the regional language before age ten. Yet in most Darnesian families in the valley, Darnesian is still spoken at home three or more generations after immigration.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: The regional language and Darnesian share a substantial portion of their vocabulary.
Children from most other immigrant groups in the valley also become fluent in the regional language before age ten.
Immigration from Darnesia to the valley began earlier than immigration from most other countries.
Many Darnesian families in the valley use the regional language when speaking with their neighbors.
Religious and civic life in the valley's Darnesian community is conducted almost entirely in Darnesian, so that taking part in it requires fluency in that language.
questions.explanation: E identifies a strong, continuing incentive for Darnesian families to keep their language alive at home, which explains why the usual pattern does not hold for them. A is the most tempting wrong answer, but shared vocabulary would make the regional language easier to adopt and gives no reason Darnesian would persist. B and D only deepen the puzzle, and C is irrelevant.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Early regional-language fluency usually kills the ancestral language at home within two generations, and Darnesian kids almost all get fluent before ten, but Darnesian is still spoken at home three-plus generations later.

breakdown.analysis: Darnesian families meet the condition that normally erases the home language, yet the home language survives. We need something special about Darnesians that keeps their language alive despite the kids' fluency. Prephrase: a strong ongoing reason to keep speaking Darnesian. It's like kids who all learn to drive at 16 but still ride bikes because their town bans cars downtown: something specific keeps the old habit useful.

choices.note: Tempting because it's about Darnesian specifically, but it points the wrong way. Shared vocabulary would make switching to the regional language easier, not give a reason to keep Darnesian.
Deepens the puzzle. If other groups also get fluent early, and their languages disappear, Darnesians look even more unusual. No explanation.
Irrelevant. Arriving earlier means more time has passed, which would if anything give the language more time to disappear. It says nothing about why it persists.
Deepens the puzzle. Using the regional language with neighbors is more pressure to switch, not a reason to keep Darnesian at home.
CORRECT. If community religious and civic life runs in Darnesian, families have a constant, practical reason to keep it fluent at home. That's the special factor that breaks the usual pattern.

questions.stimulus: Geologist: Every major earthquake recorded along the Sarn Fault in the past century was preceded, in the weeks before it struck, by a swarm of small tremors. Over the past two weeks, monitoring stations have detected a swarm along the Sarn Fault that closely matches those earlier swarms in both the frequency and the intensity of its tremors. Since the current swarm is in every measurable respect like those that came before major earthquakes, a major earthquake along the fault is imminent.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the geologist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: relies on a record of the fault's activity that is too short to reveal its behavior over geological time
takes the fact that every event of one kind was preceded by an event of a second kind to show that events of the second kind are reliably followed by events of the first kind
presumes, without providing justification, that swarms of small tremors are what cause major earthquakes along the fault
fails to consider that earthquakes along other faults might not be preceded by swarms of small tremors
draws a conclusion about the timing of an earthquake from evidence that bears only on its likely magnitude
questions.explanation: The premises show that major quakes have always followed swarms, not that swarms have always been followed by major quakes; if swarms like this one often fade without a major quake, the conclusion fails (B). C is the main trap: the argument treats swarms only as a warning sign, and its reasoning would be equally flawed whether or not swarms cause quakes. A is tempting, but a longer record would not repair the logical gap, and D and E misdescribe the argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: A major earthquake along the Sarn Fault is imminent.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Every major quake there in the past century was preceded by a tremor swarm; the current swarm matches those earlier swarms in frequency and intensity.

breakdown.analysis: Conditional reversal. The premise: major quake → swarm before it. The conclusion treats it as: swarm → major quake follows. But maybe swarms happen all the time and usually fizzle. It's like saying: every time I've had the flu, I had a sore throat first; I have a sore throat now, so I'm getting the flu. Lots of sore throats are just sore throats.

choices.note: Tempting, but more data wouldn't fix anything. Even a thousand years of "quakes follow swarms" wouldn't tell you swarms are followed by quakes. The gap is logical, not a sample-size problem.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The river hasn't flooded in the twelve years I've lived here, so it never floods.

choices.note: CORRECT. The evidence is quake → preceded by swarm. The conclusion needs swarm → followed by quake. That's exactly the reversal B describes.
Trap. The argument treats swarms as a warning sign, not a cause. And the logic would be just as broken if swarms did cause quakes, because we still don't know that every swarm leads to one.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Smoke alarms go off before houses burn down, so smoke alarms must cause house fires.

choices.note: Other faults are irrelevant. The argument is only about the Sarn Fault and its own history.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Swarms preceded every quake on the Sarn Fault, so swarms must precede quakes on every fault in the world.

choices.note: Misdescribes the argument. The swarms are matched on frequency and intensity, and the conclusion is about a major quake being imminent. There's no confusion of timing with magnitude.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: These tremors are unusually strong, so the big quake will hit tomorrow.

questions.stimulus: Legal scholar: A police officer who stops a vehicle for a traffic violation may extend the stop to investigate some other crime only if, during the stop, the officer observes something that specifically indicates that the particular vehicle or its occupants are involved in that crime. Information that merely describes a category of people or vehicles does not meet this standard, nor does anything the officer learns only after the stop has been extended.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated by the legal scholar?
choices: Officer Holt extended a traffic stop to search for contraband because the car was a model frequently used by smugglers in the region; the extension was proper.
Officer Ruiz extended a traffic stop without observing anything suspicious, but the subsequent search turned up stolen property; the extension was therefore proper.
Officer Lind stopped a car for a broken taillight and released the driver after issuing a ticket, even though she had seen a weapon on the seat; Lind acted improperly.
Officer Pratt extended a traffic stop solely because he had a strong feeling that the driver was hiding something, though nothing he observed indicated this; the extension was improper.
Officer Sato extended a traffic stop after noticing a strong smell of a controlled substance coming from the car; because of this observation, the extension was proper.
questions.explanation: The principle states a necessary condition for extending a stop; Pratt observed nothing specific, so the condition was not met and the extension was improper (D). E is the trap: Sato's observation meets the necessary condition, but the principle never says that meeting it makes an extension proper. A relies on category information, B on what was learned afterward, and C concerns an obligation to extend, which the principle never imposes.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Officer may extend a traffic stop to investigate another crime → during the stop, the officer observed something specifically indicating this vehicle/occupants are involved. Category descriptions don't count; things learned after extending don't count. Contrapositive: no specific observation during the stop → extension improper.

breakdown.analysis: This is a necessary condition only. It can tell you an extension was improper (no specific observation), but it can never tell you one was proper, because meeting a necessary condition isn't enough. So hunt for an answer that says "improper" because the officer observed nothing specific. It's like "you can enter the club only if you're 21." A 19-year-old must be turned away; a 25-year-old isn't guaranteed entry.

choices.note: The car model is category information ("a model frequently used by smugglers"), which the principle says doesn't count. And the principle can't make an extension proper anyway.

Uses what was learned after the extension, which the principle explicitly excludes. Finding stolen property afterward can't justify the extension. Also concludes "proper," which this principle never supports.
The principle limits when officers may extend. It never says they must. So it can't call Lind's choice not to extend improper.
CORRECT. A strong feeling isn't an observation, and Pratt observed nothing indicating anything. The necessary condition isn't met, so the extension was improper. That's the contrapositive in action.

Trap. The smell probably satisfies the necessary condition, but meeting a necessary condition doesn't make something proper. The principle only says when an extension is not allowed. It never says when it is.

questions.stimulus: At Brightway grocery stores, items placed on shelves at eye level sell, on average, about 30 percent more units than identical items placed on the bottom shelf. Brightway charges outside suppliers a fee for eye-level placement of their products. Last year, Brightway raised the price of its own store-brand oat cereal by 10 percent and at the same time moved the cereal from the bottom shelf to eye level. Unit sales of the cereal for the year were 5 percent higher than for the previous year.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Suppliers who pay Brightway for eye-level placement gain more from the placement than they pay in fees.
At Brightway, raising the price of an item by 10 percent typically reduces its unit sales by about 25 percent.
Had Brightway moved its store-brand cereal to eye level without raising its price, the cereal's unit sales would probably have risen by more than 5 percent.
The price increase caused Brightway's revenue from its store-brand cereal to fall last year.
Customers who buy Brightway's store-brand cereal are less sensitive to price than customers who buy other brands of cereal.
questions.explanation: Eye-level placement typically raises unit sales by about 30 percent, yet the cereal gained only 5 percent, so something, most plausibly the price increase, held sales down; without it, sales would probably have risen more (C). B is the strongest trap, but it turns one item's result into a precise rule for all items. D is unsupported: with a higher price and more units sold, revenue very likely rose. A and E go beyond the information.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. At Brightway, eye-level items sell about 30% more units on average than identical bottom-shelf items; 2. Brightway charges suppliers a fee for eye-level placement; 3. Last year Brightway raised its store-brand oat cereal price 10% and moved it from bottom shelf to eye level; 4. The cereal's unit sales rose 5% for the year.

breakdown.analysis: Do the math. The move to eye level alone typically buys about +30%. The cereal got only +5%. So something dragged it down, and the obvious candidate is the 10% price hike that happened at the same time. Supported inference: without the price hike, sales would probably have grown more than 5%. It's like getting a raise but your take-home barely moves because taxes went up at the same time: no tax hike, more take-home. Note the hedge: the right answer says "probably," which matches how strong the evidence is.

choices.note: Goes beyond the facts. We know placement boosts sales, but nothing about how big the fees are or what suppliers earn. Can't compare gain to fee.

Trap. It does the math too literally and turns one product's result into a precise rule for all items. One cereal, one year, with other things possibly going on, can't support "typically reduces sales by 25%." Too specific and too general at once.

CORRECT. Eye-level placement normally adds about 30%; the cereal added only 5% while its price went up. Without the price increase, sales would probably have risen more. The hedged "probably" fits the evidence.
Unsupported and probably false. The price went up 10% and units went up 5%, so revenue from the cereal very likely rose. Nothing suggests it fell.
No information about other brands' customers at all. If anything, the cereal's muted response hints its buyers are somewhat price sensitive. Out of scope.

questions.stimulus: Under the Fenwick zoning code, no structure taller than 12 meters may be built in a residential district unless the zoning board grants it a variance. The board may grant a variance only to a structure that either is a public utility or has been shown by its applicant to cast no shadow on any neighboring property for more than two hours per day. Grace Hill Chapel, which is in a residential district, has applied to build an 18-meter bell tower, which is not a public utility. Therefore, the chapel will not be permitted to build the tower.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: The zoning board has never granted a variance to any structure taller than 15 meters.
If the bell tower would cast a shadow on a neighboring property for more than two hours per day, the board will not grant it a variance.
Only public utilities may be granted variances without a showing about the shadows they cast.
Some of the chapel's neighbors have objected that the tower would shade their homes for much of the day.
If an applicant can show that a structure will cast no shadow on any neighboring property for more than two hours per day, then that structure is no more than 15 meters tall.
questions.explanation: By contraposition, E means no one can make the required shadow showing for an 18-meter structure; since the tower is not a public utility, it cannot get a variance and so cannot be built. A is the strongest trap, but what the board has done in the past does not guarantee what it may do now. B is a true conditional whose condition is never established, C merely restates the code, and D is irrelevant.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The chapel will not be permitted to build its 18-meter bell tower.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Residential AND over 12 m → built only with a variance; variance → public utility OR applicant shows no shadow on neighbors more than 2 hrs/day; the tower is 18 m, in a residential district, and not a public utility.

breakdown.analysis: Chain: Built → variance → utility OR shadow showing. Not a utility, so we need: no shadow showing possible. The premises never say the chapel can't make that showing. Missing link: an 18-m structure can't be shown to cast so little shadow. E gives it: shadow showing → ≤15 m. Contrapositive: over 15 m → no shadow showing. Tower is 18 m → no showing → (not a utility) → no variance → not built. It's like "you can enter only with a ticket or a pass; you have no pass" and then you need a rule that guarantees you can't have a ticket.

choices.note: Trap. A past record isn't a rule. "The board has never done it" doesn't mean it can't now. The conclusion still doesn't follow with certainty.
A fine conditional, but its trigger is never established: we don't know the tower would cast that much shadow. Without that, B never kicks in.
Just a restatement of the code's rule. It adds nothing about whether the chapel can make the shadow showing, which is the missing piece.
Neighbors objecting isn't the standard. The question is whether the applicant can show limited shadow. Complaints don't guarantee the showing fails.

CORRECT. Contrapositive: taller than 15 m → can't show limited shadow. 18 m tower → no shadow showing; not a utility → no variance; residential and over 12 m with no variance → can't be built. The conclusion is now guaranteed.

questions.stimulus: Public health officials in Merrow County attribute this year's decline in measles cases in the county to the vaccination campaign they launched last winter. Admittedly, the number of measles cases nationwide has also declined this year, which might suggest that the county's decline merely reflects a broader trend. But the county's decline began within a month of the campaign's launch and was nearly three times as steep as the national decline. So the officials' attribution is probably correct.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the argument by the claim that the number of measles cases nationwide has also declined this year?
choices: It is cited as a consideration that might be taken to count against the argument's conclusion.
It is the conclusion that the argument as a whole is intended to support.
It is offered as evidence that directly supports the officials' attribution.
It is a subsidiary conclusion that is used to support the argument's main conclusion.
It is a claim that the argument ultimately attempts to show is false.
questions.explanation: Introduced by 'Admittedly,' the national decline is a concession that might suggest a broader trend rather than the campaign explains the county's decline (A). E is the trap: the argument accepts that cases fell nationwide and rejects only the inference drawn from that fact. C reverses the claim's bearing, and the claim is neither the main nor a subsidiary conclusion (B, D).

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The officials' attribution of the county's measles decline to their vaccination campaign is probably correct.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Concession: cases also fell nationwide, which might suggest a broader trend; reply: the county decline began within a month of the campaign and was nearly three times as steep as the national decline.

breakdown.analysis: "Admittedly" flags a concession: a point that seems to cut against the conclusion, which the author grants and then answers. The national decline might make you think the county is just riding a wave. The author accepts the fact and argues it doesn't explain the timing or the steepness. Role: a consideration that could count against the conclusion. It's like: "Sure, everyone's grades went up this year. But mine jumped right after I got a tutor, and three times as much."

choices.note: CORRECT. "Admittedly" introduces it, and the author says it "might suggest that the county's decline merely reflects a broader trend." That's a consideration against the conclusion, which the author then answers.
The main conclusion is that the officials' attribution is probably correct. The national decline is something the author has to deal with, not the point being proved.
Opposite. The national decline cuts against the officials' attribution, which is why the author has to rebut it. It's not support.
Not a conclusion of any kind. Nothing supports it within the argument; it's simply a fact the author concedes.

Trap. The author never says the national decline didn't happen. The author accepts the fact and rejects only the inference that it explains the county's drop. Granting a fact is not trying to prove it false.

questions.stimulus: Studio executive: Over the past year, screenings in our chain's few premium large-format auditoriums have generated far more revenue per screening than screenings of the very same films in our standard auditoriums. Premium screenings cost little more to run than standard ones. So if we convert half of our standard auditoriums to the premium large format, our total box-office revenue will increase substantially.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the executive's argument?
choices: The films shown in the chain's premium auditoriums are almost all major releases, which draw large audiences in any format.
Some moviegoers prefer standard auditoriums because they find large-format screens uncomfortably bright.
Converting a standard auditorium to the premium large format requires closing it for several weeks.
Demand for premium large-format screenings is already nearly fully met by the chain's existing premium auditoriums, which seldom sell out.
Several competing theater chains have recently converted some of their auditoriums to the premium large format.
questions.explanation: The executive assumes that new premium auditoriums would earn what the existing ones earn; if current premium capacity already meets demand, added premium screenings would largely draw patrons away from standard ones or go unfilled (D). A is the trap: the comparison already concerns the very same films in both formats, so the films' popularity cannot explain the difference. C describes only a temporary loss, B concerns only some patrons, and E's effect is unclear.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Converting half the standard auditoriums to premium large format will substantially increase total box-office revenue.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The chain's few premium auditoriums earn far more per screening than standard screenings of the same films; premium screenings cost little more to run.

breakdown.analysis: The executive assumes new premium screens would perform like the current few. But the current ones might be skimming all the premium demand there is. Add a lot more and they may sit half-empty or just steal customers from the standard rooms. It's like a food truck that sells out every lunch, so the owner buys ten more trucks, without asking if there are ten trucks' worth of hungry people. Prephrase: there isn't enough extra demand for many more premium screenings.

choices.note: Trap. The comparison is already the very same films in both formats, so big releases are on both sides. Film popularity can't explain why premium earns more per screening.
"Some" moviegoers is small. Half the standard rooms would remain, so these people still have options. Doesn't seriously threaten the revenue increase.
A few weeks of closure is a temporary cost. The conclusion is about revenue increasing substantially going forward, which a short shutdown doesn't undercut.

CORRECT. If existing premium rooms already nearly meet demand and seldom sell out, new premium screens won't fill. They'll mostly pull patrons from standard rooms or run with empty seats. The per-screening advantage won't carry over.
Unclear effect. Competitors converting might steal premium customers, or might show premium is popular. Either way it's weaker and less direct than D.

questions.stimulus: Some linguists claim that the Orvic language must have borrowed its words for metals from the neighboring Talesh language, because the Orvic and Talesh words for 'iron,' 'copper,' and 'tin' are strikingly similar. But similarity runs in both directions. If the similarity of these words shows that Orvic borrowed them from Talesh, it shows equally well that Talesh borrowed them from Orvic. Similarity alone, therefore, cannot establish which language did the borrowing.
questions.stem: The argument proceeds by
choices: arguing that the similarity of the words is more likely the result of chance than of borrowing
pointing out that the evidence offered for a claim would equally support a competing claim
arguing that the linguists' claim is false on the grounds that the evidence offered for it is inadequate
drawing a general conclusion about all languages from the features of only two of them
questioning the accuracy of the data the linguists used in comparing the two languages
questions.explanation: The argument shows that the cited similarity supports Talesh borrowing from Orvic just as well as the reverse, so it cannot decide between them (B). C is the trap: the argument concludes only that similarity cannot establish the direction of borrowing, not that Orvic did not borrow from Talesh. A misreads the argument, which grants the similarity and never appeals to chance, and the argument neither generalizes (D) nor disputes the data (E).

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Similarity alone can't establish which language borrowed metal words from the other.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Some linguists say Orvic borrowed from Talesh because the words are similar; but similarity runs both ways, so it supports Talesh borrowing from Orvic just as well.

breakdown.analysis: The author doesn't say the linguists are wrong. They say the evidence is symmetric: whatever it shows for "Orvic borrowed," it shows equally for "Talesh borrowed." So it can't pick between them. It's like saying "my brother and I look alike, so I must take after him" when it shows just as well that he takes after you.

choices.note: The author never appeals to chance. The similarity is granted and treated as consistent with borrowing; the issue is direction.
choices.example: Example of this method: These two words look alike, but with thousands of words in each language, a few lookalikes are bound to happen by coincidence.

choices.note: CORRECT. The author shows the linguists' evidence (similarity) supports the competing claim (Talesh borrowed from Orvic) equally well. That's exactly B.
Trap. The author concludes only that similarity can't establish the direction, not that Orvic didn't borrow from Talesh. Insufficient evidence for a claim doesn't make the claim false.
choices.example: Example of this method: The linguists' only evidence that Orvic borrowed from Talesh is weak, so Orvic did not borrow from Talesh.

choices.note: There's no generalization to all languages. The argument is about Orvic and Talesh and one kind of evidence.
choices.example: Example of this method: Orvic and Talesh share metal words, so all neighboring languages share their metal words.

choices.note: The author accepts the data: the words really are similar. The objection is to what that data proves.
choices.example: Example of this method: The linguists claim the words are similar, but their transcriptions of the Talesh words are full of errors.

questions.stimulus: Project manager: Our engineers estimate that rewriting the billing module in a newer programming language would take a team six months. But the module consists of twelve components, and the engineers agree that any one of those components could be rewritten by a single engineer in about two weeks. So if we assign a different engineer to each of the twelve components, the entire rewrite should take only about two weeks.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the project manager's argument is flawed in that it
choices: relies on estimates made by engineers who may have an interest in the outcome of the project
presumes without justification that the newer programming language is superior to the current one
presumes that what is true of the engineers as a group must be true of each engineer individually
takes for granted that a rewrite should be undertaken if it can be completed quickly
fails to consider that rewriting a whole may require work beyond rewriting each of its parts separately
questions.explanation: The components presumably have to be made to work together, so rewriting the whole can take longer than rewriting each part in isolation; the manager ignores this, along with the engineers' six-month estimate (E). C is the trap but reverses the error: the manager reasons from parts to a whole, not from a group to its members. A attacks the source rather than the reasoning, and B and D describe reasoning the manager never uses.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: With one engineer per component, the whole billing rewrite should take about two weeks.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Engineers estimate a team needs six months; the module has twelve components; each component could be rewritten by one engineer in about two weeks.

breakdown.analysis: Part-to-whole error. Rewriting each piece in isolation isn't the same as rewriting the whole system: the pieces have to fit together, be tested together, and work together. The engineers' own six-month estimate is a big hint that integration takes real time. It's like saying twelve people can each bake one layer of a wedding cake in an hour, so the whole cake is done in an hour, ignoring stacking, frosting, and making the layers line up.

choices.note: Attacks the source, not the reasoning, and there's no hint the engineers have a stake. Plus the manager actually ignores their main estimate, so this isn't the problem.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The engineers say the rewrite will take six months, but they get paid by the hour, so the real number must be shorter.

choices.note: Nothing about whether the new language is better. The argument is only about how long the rewrite takes.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: We should rewrite the module in the new language because it's newer, so it must be better.

choices.note: Trap, and it runs the wrong way. The manager reasons from parts (components) to the whole (module), not from a group to its individual members.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The engineering team is very experienced, so each engineer on it must be very experienced.

choices.note: The manager never argues the rewrite should happen. The argument is only a time estimate.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The rewrite can be done in two weeks, so we should definitely do it.

choices.note: CORRECT. The whole may require more than the sum of the parts: integrating, testing, and coordinating twelve rewritten components. The manager ignores that, and ignores the engineers' six-month estimate that likely reflects it.

questions.stimulus: The cave at Morrin Hollow contains stalagmites whose growth layers record past rainfall: layers formed during wetter periods are thicker than those formed during drier periods. The researchers studying the cave confirmed that its air temperature has stayed essentially constant for at least a thousand years. Because the layers formed over the most recent four centuries are on average much thinner than those formed in the preceding centuries, the researchers conclude that the region has been considerably drier during the past four hundred years than it was before.
questions.stem: Which one of the following would it be most useful to know in order to evaluate the researchers' argument?
choices: whether the temperature inside other caves in the region has also remained constant
whether the region has become wetter during the most recent few decades
whether the amount of water that seeps into the cave from the surface depends on anything other than the amount of rain that falls
whether thick growth layers have been found in stalagmites from caves in wetter regions
whether wetter periods in the region have also tended to be warmer than drier periods
questions.explanation: The argument takes thinner layers as a sign of less rain; if seepage into the cave depends on other things, such as vegetation or soil above the cave, those could have changed four centuries ago and thinned the layers without any drop in rainfall (C). B is the trap: a recent wet spell would barely affect a four-century average and would not show whether the layers track rainfall. A concerns other caves, the researchers have already addressed temperature (E), and D merely restates what the premises already grant.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The region has been considerably drier over the past 400 years than before.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Stalagmite layers are thicker in wetter periods; cave temperature has been constant for 1,000+ years; layers from the last four centuries are much thinner on average.

breakdown.analysis: The argument treats layer thickness as a rain gauge. They've ruled out temperature. But thickness depends on how much water drips into the cave, and that might depend on things besides rainfall: soil, vegetation, land use above the cave. If any of those changed 400 years ago, thinner layers wouldn't mean less rain. It's like judging how much it rained by how full your rain barrel is, without checking whether someone moved the gutter. An evaluate answer is a question whose answer would swing the argument either way.

choices.note: Other caves are irrelevant. The argument depends on this cave's temperature, which is already confirmed constant.
Trap. A few recent wet decades barely move a four-century average and don't tell us whether layer thickness actually tracks rainfall. Either answer leaves the argument about where it was.

CORRECT. If seepage depends only on rain, thin layers really do mean less rain and the argument is strong. If it depends on other factors (soil, plants, land use above the cave), those could explain the thinning and the argument falls apart.
The premises already tell us wetter periods produce thicker layers. Knowing this about other caves just repeats a granted premise.
The researchers already confirmed the cave's temperature hasn't changed, so whether wetter periods outside were warmer doesn't affect how this cave's layers formed.

questions.stimulus: In the state of Varnell, eyewitnesses used to view police lineups administered by the detective investigating the case. Five years ago the state began requiring that lineups be administered by an officer who does not know which person in the lineup is the suspect. Since then, the proportion of eyewitnesses who pick a 'filler', a lineup member known to be innocent, has risen, while the proportion who pick the suspect has fallen. Researchers conclude that under the old procedure, detectives' knowledge was subtly steering witnesses toward the suspect.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the researchers' argument?
choices: In laboratory studies using lineups in which no member had committed the staged crime, witnesses more often chose the member designated as the suspect when the administrator knew of that designation than when the administrator did not.
Detectives in Varnell generally opposed the new requirement when it was first proposed.
Over the past five years, the average time between a crime and the lineup at which a witness views a suspect has increased substantially in Varnell.
Witnesses who pick a filler from a lineup are rarely called to testify at trial.
Several other states adopted the same requirement at around the same time Varnell did.
questions.explanation: A shows, under controlled conditions where witness memory cannot explain the result, that an administrator's knowledge alone can steer witnesses toward a designated person, which is the mechanism the researchers propose. C is the trap: longer delays could weaken witnesses' memories and account for more filler picks without any steering, so C weakens the argument. B, D, and E do not bear on why the pattern of identifications changed.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Under the old procedure, detectives' knowledge subtly steered witnesses toward the suspect.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Five years ago Varnell began requiring lineup administrators who don't know who the suspect is; since then, filler picks rose and suspect picks fell.

breakdown.analysis: A before/after change, explained by one cause: the administrator's knowledge. To strengthen, either rule out other explanations for the shift or show the proposed mechanism actually works. The best help is direct proof that an administrator who knows the suspect makes witnesses pick that person. It's like believing a poker player has a tell: it helps a lot to run a test where you know the cards and watch whether people read his face.

choices.note: CORRECT. In lineups where nobody is guilty, so witness memory can't explain the choice, witnesses picked the "suspect" more when the administrator knew who it was. That's the steering mechanism, demonstrated directly.
Detectives' opinions about the rule tell us nothing about whether their knowledge steered witnesses. Maybe they opposed it for cost or convenience.
Trap, and it weakens. Longer delays fade memories, which could explain more filler picks and fewer suspect picks without any steering. That's an alternate cause.
What happens at trial is irrelevant to why identification patterns changed at the lineup.
Other states adopting the rule doesn't show it changed anything or that steering happened. If it said those states saw the same shift, it might help, but it doesn't.

questions.stimulus: Retail analyst: Our review of the Calloway grocery chain's results for last year shows two things. Most of the Calloway chain's stores that introduced a customer loyalty program last year saw their profits rise. And most of the chain's stores whose profits rose last year are located in suburban shopping centers. It follows that at least some of the Calloway stores that introduced a loyalty program last year are located in suburban shopping centers.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the analyst's argument?
choices: Most of the orchard's trees that were pruned in winter produced heavy crops, and most of the orchard's trees that were pruned in winter are apple trees. So at least some of the orchard's apple trees produced heavy crops.
Most of the library branches that extended their hours saw circulation rise, and no downtown branch saw circulation rise. So at least some of the branches that extended their hours are not downtown.
Most of the paintings the museum restored last year are landscapes. So most of the landscapes in the museum were restored last year.

Most of the guild's apprentices who completed the advanced course passed the certification exam, and most of the guild's apprentices who passed the exam later opened their own workshops. So at least some apprentices who completed the advanced course later opened their own workshops.
Most of the restaurants on Fell Street that serve breakfast are profitable. The Juniper restaurant on Fell Street serves breakfast. So the Juniper restaurant must be profitable.
questions.explanation: The analyst chains two 'most' statements whose middle groups differ (most A are B; most B are C), which does not guarantee any overlap between A and C, since the B's that are A may be exactly the B's that are not C; D repeats this error. A is the main trap: both of its 'most' statements are about the same group of pruned trees, so the two majorities must overlap and the reasoning is valid. B is also valid, C commits a different error (reversing 'most'), and E turns 'most' into certainty.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: At least some Calloway stores that introduced a loyalty program are in suburban shopping centers.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most loyalty-program stores saw profits rise; most stores whose profits rose are suburban.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Most A are B; most B are C; so some A are C. (Flawed: the two "most" statements have different subjects, so the A's among the B's could all be in the non-C minority.)

breakdown.analysis: Two "most" statements only guarantee overlap when they're about the same group. Here one is about loyalty stores, the other about profit-rise stores. Counterexample: 10 loyalty stores, 6 had profits rise. But 100 stores total had profits rise, and 60 of those are suburban. The 6 loyalty stores could all be among the 40 non-suburban ones. Find the answer with "most A are B, most B are C, so some A are C."

choices.note: Trap. Both "most" statements are about the same group: winter-pruned trees. Most of them had heavy crops and most of them are apple trees, so those majorities must overlap. This is valid, unlike the analyst's argument.

Valid reasoning. Most extended-hours branches saw a rise; no downtown branch saw a rise; so those rising branches aren't downtown. That guarantees some extended-hours branches aren't downtown. No flaw to match.
A different flaw: reversing a "most." Most restored paintings are landscapes doesn't mean most landscapes were restored. Flawed, but not the same pattern.

CORRECT. Most course-completers passed; most passers opened workshops; so some completers opened workshops. Most A are B, most B are C, so some A are C, with the same gap: the completers who passed could all be in the passers' minority who didn't open shops.
A different flaw: going from "most" to a certainty about one member. Juniper could be in the unprofitable minority. Not the two-most chain.

questions.stimulus: A study of commuters in the city of Arlow found that those who regularly cycled to work had significantly lower rates of heart disease than those who drove to work. The researchers adjusted their results for differences in income and smoking habits and concluded that cycling to work reduces the risk of heart disease. But this conclusion is not warranted, since the cyclists in the study were, on average, considerably younger than the drivers, and the researchers made no adjustment for age.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
choices: Cycling to work does nothing to reduce a commuter's risk of heart disease.
Among Arlow commuters, greater age is associated with at least some increase in the risk of heart disease.
The difference in average age between the cyclists and the drivers is large enough to account for the entire difference in their rates of heart disease.
Age has a greater effect on the risk of heart disease than either income or smoking habits does.
The cyclists in the study had not been cycling to work long enough for it to affect their health.
questions.explanation: The objection works only if the age gap could account for at least part of the difference in heart disease rates; if older commuters were at no greater risk, the younger age of the cyclists would not bias the result in the researchers' favor (B). C is the main trap: to show the conclusion unwarranted, the argument needs age to be a possible explanation, not the complete one. A is likewise too strong, since the argument does not claim cycling has no benefit, and D and E are not needed.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The researchers' conclusion that cycling to work reduces heart-disease risk isn't warranted.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The cyclists were on average considerably younger than the drivers, and the researchers didn't adjust for age.

breakdown.analysis: The author points to age as an uncontrolled factor. That objection only matters if age is linked to heart disease at all. If older commuters weren't any more at risk, the age gap would be harmless and the objection would fizzle. The author doesn't need age to explain the whole difference, just to be a possible part of it. It's like objecting that a study of tall vs. short basketball players ignored shoe brand: that's only a problem if shoe brand affects scoring.

choices.note: Too strong. The author says the conclusion isn't warranted, not that it's false. Cycling could help and the study still be flawed. Negating it doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: Cycling to work does at least something to reduce a commuter's risk of heart disease.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it and the objection dies: if age has no link to heart-disease risk, the cyclists being younger doesn't bias the result, and the uncontrolled age difference is no reason to doubt the conclusion.
choices.negation: Among Arlow commuters, greater age is not associated with any increase in the risk of heart disease.

choices.note: Trap. Too strong. To call a conclusion unwarranted, the author needs age to be a possible explanation for part of the gap, not the whole thing. Negating it (age explains only some) still leaves the objection standing.
choices.negation: The difference in average age is not large enough to account for the entire difference in heart-disease rates.

choices.note: Not needed. Age doesn't have to beat income or smoking; it just has to matter somewhat. Negating it doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: Age does not have a greater effect on heart-disease risk than both income and smoking habits do.

choices.note: Not needed, and it would argue that cycling had no effect, which goes beyond the author's point. Negating it doesn't hurt the age objection.
choices.negation: The cyclists in the study had been cycling to work long enough for it to affect their health.

questions.stimulus: The Linden Park neighborhood association argues that the city should deny a permit for a homeless shelter on Cobb Street because property values near shelters sometimes decline. But the shelter would meet a pressing public need that cannot be met elsewhere: no other available site in the city lies within walking distance of both the public hospital and the central transit hub, on which the shelter's residents depend. And any decline in nearby property values would likely be small. So the city should grant the permit.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the reasoning above?
choices: A city should never deny a permit for a proposed land use merely because nearby residents object to it.
A city should grant a permit for a proposed land use whenever that use would impose no costs on nearby property owners.
A permit should be denied whenever a proposed land use would lower nearby property values, unless the need that the use serves could not be met at any other site.
Facilities that serve the public should, whenever possible, be located within walking distance of hospitals and transit hubs.

A city should deny a permit for a proposed land use that meets an important public need only if that need could be met at another site or the use would impose substantial costs on nearby property owners.
questions.explanation: E's contrapositive says that when a use meets an important need that cannot be met elsewhere and imposes no substantial costs, the permit should not be denied, which matches the argument's premises and yields its conclusion. C is the hardest trap: when no other site is available, it removes one requirement to deny, but it never says the permit should be granted. B does not apply because the argument concedes some decline in property values is likely, and A and D do not connect the premises to the conclusion.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The city should grant the permit for the Cobb Street shelter.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The shelter meets a pressing public need that can't be met elsewhere (no other site is near both the hospital and the transit hub); any drop in nearby property values would likely be small.

breakdown.analysis: A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says. The conclusion is "grant," or at least "don't deny." The premises give us: important need, can't be met elsewhere, costs to neighbors small. So we want a rule like: important need + no other site + no substantial costs → don't deny. E says deny only if (other site OR substantial costs). Contrapositive: no other site AND no substantial costs → don't deny. Both conditions are met, so: don't deny, i.e., grant. It's like a rule "you may cut someone from the team only if they skip practice or break rules": a player who does neither can't be cut.

choices.note: Doesn't connect the premises to the conclusion. The argument isn't about residents merely objecting; it's about need and costs. And "don't deny for this one reason" isn't "grant."
Requires no costs at all. The argument concedes there will likely be some small decline in property values, so B's condition isn't met and it never applies.
Hardest trap. With no other site available, C's requirement to deny is switched off. But turning off a reason to deny isn't a reason to grant. C never tells the city to grant anything.
A siting preference, not a permit rule. It says nothing about whether this permit should be granted over the neighbors' concern.

CORRECT. Deny → other site OR substantial costs. Contrapositive: no other site AND no substantial costs → don't deny. The premises supply both (no other site; decline would be small), so the city shouldn't deny: grant the permit.

questions.stimulus: In every dialect spoken on the Kessavan islands, words borrowed from the mainland language are always stressed on the first syllable, whatever their stress in the mainland language. Native Kessavan words, by contrast, are stressed on the first syllable only when that syllable contains a long vowel. A linguist recorded a lifelong resident of Ollo, one of the Kessavan islands, speaking the Ollo dialect. The speaker pronounced the word 'tamesh' with stress on the second syllable. The first syllable of 'tamesh' contains a short vowel.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: 'Tamesh' is a native Kessavan word.
'Tamesh' is not stressed on its first syllable in any Kessavan dialect.
'Tamesh,' as used in the Ollo dialect, is not a word that the dialect borrowed from the mainland language.
Every native Kessavan word whose first syllable contains a short vowel is stressed on the second syllable.
Any Kessavan word that is stressed on the first syllable is a word borrowed from the mainland language.
questions.explanation: Mainland borrowings are stressed on the first syllable in every Kessavan dialect, and 'tamesh' was stressed on the second syllable in the Ollo dialect, so in that dialect it is not a mainland borrowing (C). A is the main trap: 'tamesh' could have been borrowed from some third language, which the stimulus says nothing about. B fails for the same reason, since the stress pattern of words from other sources, or in other dialects, is unknown. D overreaches (stress could fall on a later syllable), and E ignores native words with long first vowels.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. In every Kessavan dialect, mainland borrowings are always stressed on the first syllable; 2. Native Kessavan words are stressed on the first syllable only when it has a long vowel; 3. A lifelong Ollo resident, speaking Ollo dialect, stressed 'tamesh' on the second syllable; 4. The first syllable of 'tamesh' has a short vowel.

breakdown.analysis: Mainland borrowing → stressed on first syllable. 'Tamesh' in Ollo is not stressed on the first syllable. Contrapositive: so in Ollo it isn't a mainland borrowing. That's all we can safely say. We can't say it's native: words might come from somewhere else entirely. It's like: every employee badge is blue; this badge is red; so it's not an employee badge. That doesn't make it a visitor badge; it could be a contractor's.

choices.note: Trap. The facts only cover two categories: mainland borrowings and native words. 'Tamesh' could come from some third language. Ruling out "mainland" doesn't make it native.
We only have one dialect's pronunciation. If 'tamesh' came from another source, or is pronounced differently elsewhere, other dialects could stress the first syllable. Unsupported.

CORRECT. Mainland borrowings are always first-syllable stressed in every dialect. In Ollo, 'tamesh' was stressed on the second syllable. So in Ollo, it isn't a mainland borrowing. Note how carefully it's limited to the Ollo dialect.
Overreaches. Native short-vowel words aren't stressed on the first syllable, but that doesn't mean the second. Stress could fall on the third or later.
False by the facts: native words with a long first vowel are stressed on the first syllable too. First-syllable stress doesn't prove a borrowing.

questions.stimulus: Film archivist: Any film restored using the Calder process has lost some of its original color information. No film can be included in our archive's 'authentic presentation' series unless it retains all of its original color information. Every nitrate film in the Vantor collection was restored either by the Calder process or by our archive's own laboratory. The Gilded Gate is one of the nitrate films in the Vantor collection. Therefore, The Gilded Gate cannot be included in the authentic presentation series.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if assumed, enables the archivist's conclusion to be properly drawn?
choices: Any film that retains all of its original color information was not restored by the archive's own laboratory.
Every film that has been restored using the Calder process is a nitrate film.
The archive's own laboratory restores films using some process other than the Calder process.
Most films restored by the archive's own laboratory have lost some of their original color information.
Every film that has lost some of its original color information was restored either by the Calder process or by the archive's own laboratory.
questions.explanation: The Gilded Gate was restored either by the Calder process or by the archive's laboratory. The Calder branch already means lost color, and A, by contraposition, says every film the laboratory restored has also lost color, so either way the film is excluded. D is the closest trap, but 'most' leaves open that The Gilded Gate is a laboratory restoration that kept all its color. E reverses the needed conditional, B is irrelevant, and C does not say whether the laboratory's process loses color.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Gilded Gate cannot be included in the authentic presentation series.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Calder process → lost some color; in series → retains all color; every Vantor nitrate film was restored by Calder OR the archive's lab; The Gilded Gate is a Vantor nitrate film.

breakdown.analysis: Two branches. Calder branch: Calder → lost color → not in series. Done. Lab branch: we know nothing about what the lab does to color. That's the hole. We need: lab-restored → lost color. A says retains all color → not lab-restored; contrapositive: lab-restored → lost color. Now both branches end at lost color → not in series. It's like: you got here by bus or by train; the bus always makes you late; we need the train to make you late too before we can say you're late.

choices.note: CORRECT. Contrapositive: lab-restored → lost some color. So whichever branch The Gilded Gate took (Calder or lab), it lost color, and anything that lost color can't be in the series.
Irrelevant. Whether Calder films are nitrate doesn't touch the lab branch, which is the gap.
Knowing the lab uses a different process tells us nothing about whether that process loses color. The gap stays open.
Closest trap. "Most" isn't enough for a guaranteed conclusion. The Gilded Gate might be one of the lab restorations that kept all its color.
Reverses the needed direction. E says lost color → Calder or lab. We need lab → lost color. E tells us where color-losing films came from, not what happens to lab films.

questions.stimulus: Security analyst: Of the security breaches at Halvern Corporation last year, 80 percent involved employee laptops running the older version of the company's operating system, while only 20 percent involved laptops running the new version. Clearly, then, Halvern's laptops that run the older version are much more likely to be involved in a security breach than are Halvern's laptops that run the new version.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the security analyst's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: presumes, without justification, that the design of the older version is what makes the laptops that run it vulnerable to breaches
relies on data from a single year, which may not reflect the company's long-term pattern of breaches
draws a conclusion about companies in general on the basis of evidence about a single company
