treats the share of incidents that involve members of a group as though it indicated how often members of that group are involved in incidents
treats the occurrence of a breach as evidence that the breach was caused by an employee's carelessness
questions.explanation: If, say, 90 percent of Halvern's laptops run the older version, then their accounting for 80 percent of breaches would make them, if anything, less likely to be breached; the argument confuses share of breaches with rate of breaches (D). A is the main trap: the conclusion says only that older-version laptops are more likely to be involved in breaches, not why, so it makes no causal claim about the software's design. B is tempting, but a single year's data does not make the comparison itself invalid, C ignores that the conclusion concerns only Halvern, and E is not in the argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Halvern laptops on the older OS are much more likely to be breached than laptops on the new version.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: 80% of last year's breaches involved older-version laptops; 20% involved new-version laptops.

breakdown.analysis: Share vs. rate. You can't compare how likely each group is to be breached without knowing how big each group is. Suppose 90% of laptops run the old version: then old laptops are 90% of the fleet but only 80% of breaches, so they're actually less likely to be breached. It's like saying most car accidents involve sober drivers, so sober driving is more dangerous than drunk driving. Most drivers are sober.

choices.note: Trap. The conclusion only says older-version laptops are more likely to be involved in breaches. It doesn't say why, so there's no claim about the software's design.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Older-version laptops get breached more often, so the older version's code must be what lets attackers in.

choices.note: A single year is a possible weakness, but it isn't what breaks this argument. Even with ten years of the same 80/20 split, you'd still need to know how many laptops run each version.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: We had few breaches this year, so our security must be strong in general.

choices.note: Wrong scope. The conclusion is only about Halvern's laptops. No generalization to other companies.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: At Halvern, old-version laptops get breached more, so at every company old operating systems are riskier.

choices.note: CORRECT. 80% of breaches involving old-version laptops is a share of incidents. It says nothing about how often any given old-version laptop gets breached unless you know what share of the laptops run the old version.
Employee carelessness is never mentioned. The argument doesn't assign blame to anyone.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: There was a breach on Maria's laptop, so Maria must have been careless.

questions.stimulus: Geologist: Any rock sample from the Tellis formation that contains garnet must have been metamorphosed at high pressure. Analysis has shown that none of the rock samples collected at the quarry site was metamorphosed at high pressure. So none of the quarry-site samples that come from the Tellis formation contains garnet, though samples from other formations at the site might.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the geologist's argument?
choices: Every apprentice at Dunmore Builders who has completed safety training is permitted to operate the table saw. None of the workers on the Elm Street project has completed safety training. So none of the Dunmore apprentices on the Elm Street project is permitted to operate the table saw.

Every painting in the Ashby collection that is signed was authenticated by the museum's conservator. None of the paintings on loan to the Rook Gallery was authenticated by the conservator. So none of the Ashby paintings on loan to the Rook Gallery is signed.

Every seedling at the Corvo nursery that was grown from a cutting is genetically identical to its parent plant. All of the seedlings in the greenhouse are genetically identical to their parent plants. So all of the Corvo seedlings in the greenhouse were grown from cuttings.

Every bird in the Pellam reserve that nests on the ground is vulnerable to foxes. None of the birds in the eastern marsh is vulnerable to foxes. So none of the birds in the eastern marsh nests on the ground.

Some of the bridges in Ralston County that were built before 1960 need structural repairs. None of the bridges on Route 9 needs structural repairs. So none of the Ralston County bridges on Route 9 was built before 1960.
questions.explanation: The geologist validly reasons that garnet-bearing Tellis samples must show high-pressure metamorphism, no quarry sample does, and so no Tellis sample from the quarry contains garnet; B matches this exactly. D is the main trap: its conclusion covers all eastern-marsh birds, but its premise covers only Pellam birds, so unlike the original it does not limit the conclusion to the overlapping group. A denies the sufficient condition, C affirms the necessary one, and E treats 'some' as if it were 'all.'

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: None of the quarry-site samples from the Tellis formation contains garnet (samples from other formations might).

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Tellis sample with garnet → high-pressure metamorphism; no quarry sample was metamorphosed at high pressure.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Every X that is G is P; no Q is P; so no Q that is X is G. (Valid, and the conclusion is limited to things that are both X and Q.)

breakdown.analysis: This one is valid. Rule is restricted to Tellis samples. Contrapositive: no high pressure → not a garnet-bearing Tellis sample. No quarry sample had high pressure, so no quarry sample that's from Tellis has garnet. Notice the careful scoping: the conclusion only covers samples that are both Tellis and quarry. Match an answer with the same restricted rule, the same "none of group Q" premise, and the same narrowed conclusion.

choices.note: Denies the sufficient condition. Training → permitted, but no training doesn't mean not permitted. Someone could be allowed to use the saw for some other reason. Flawed, unlike the original.

CORRECT. Signed Ashby painting → authenticated. No Rook loan was authenticated. So no Ashby painting on loan to Rook is signed. Same restricted rule, same "none" premise, same narrowed conclusion. Perfect match.
Affirms the necessary condition. Cutting → identical; greenhouse seedlings are identical; so they're from cuttings. They could be identical for another reason. Flawed.

Main trap. Close, but the conclusion covers every bird in the eastern marsh, while the rule only covers Pellam birds. The original carefully limited its conclusion to the overlap (quarry samples that are Tellis). D overreaches to marsh birds outside Pellam.
Treats "some" as "all." Only some pre-1960 Ralston bridges need repairs, so a pre-1960 bridge on Route 9 could be one that doesn't. Flawed, and not the original's pattern.

passages.title: Repetition in Malek’s The Salt Ledger
passages.text:
When Teodora Malek’s final novel, The Salt Ledger, appeared in English, reviewers were nearly unanimous in their complaint: the book repeats itself. Entire sentences recur, sometimes verbatim, sometimes with a single word altered; characters are introduced with the same epithet each time they appear; and the narrator returns, at intervals that seem arbitrary, to a description of the harbor at low tide. Most critics attributed these features to the fatigue of an aging writer or to an editorial process too deferential to correct them. Such explanations, however, assume that Malek was attempting the kind of novel her earlier books had been—densely plotted, psychologically intimate realism—and fell short. A more productive assumption is that she was attempting something else entirely.

Malek grew up in the fishing villages of the Dravan coast, where, as she recounts in her memoir, evenings were given over to the recitation of long communal narratives. Those narratives were never fixed texts. A teller rebuilt each one from a stock of formulaic phrases and recurring scenes, and listeners, who already knew the outline of the story, judged a performance by how artfully the teller varied the familiar. Repetition in this setting was not redundancy but structure: a recurring phrase signaled to the audience where they stood in the tale, and a small change in a phrase they knew by heart carried more weight than any new sentence could.

Read in this light, the repetitions in The Salt Ledger become legible. The harbor passage, for instance, recurs seven times, and each recurrence alters one detail—a boat missing, a mooring line frayed—that registers the losses the village has suffered since the last telling. A reader who skims the passage as filler misses some of the novel’s most important events, which Malek deliberately refuses to narrate directly. The epithets work similarly: when the widow Anka, called “the patient one” throughout, is finally called “the patient one, still,” the single added word conveys a judgment the narrator never voices. Not every repetition yields to this reading. A few sentences in the middle chapters recur unaltered and seem to do no work at all, and it is possible that these, at least, are the lapses the critics took the whole book to be. But an interpretation need not redeem every sentence to be preferable to one that redeems none.

The English translation obscured much of this. Its translator, evidently treating the repetitions as lapses, varied the wording of recurring passages to avoid monotony, so that Malek’s small, deliberate alterations are lost among many incidental ones. It would be too much to say that the critics’ verdict was produced entirely by the translation; some reviewers who read the original voiced the same complaint. But a reader of the English edition was given little chance to notice that the book’s apparent flaws follow a pattern. What looks like a novelist losing control of her material may instead be a novelist returning, at the end of her career, to the oldest form of control she knew.
passages.subject: humanities

passages.title: Contracts made by software agents
passages.text:
Passage A

Software agents now routinely negotiate and conclude transactions on behalf of the people who deploy them: they reorder supplies, book travel, and bid in auctions, often without any human reviewing the particular terms. When such an agent strikes a bargain its user later regrets, courts must decide whether the user is bound. The answer should be yes, in nearly every case.

The traditional requirement of mutual assent is not offended by this conclusion. A person who sets an agent loose in a marketplace has manifested, by that very act, a willingness to be bound by the transactions it concludes, just as a merchant who installs a vending machine has manifested a willingness to sell at the posted price to anyone who inserts the coins. The assent is general rather than particular, but contract law has long recognized general assent; no one supposes that the vending-machine owner must approve each sale. It may be objected that a user cannot assent to a term she could not foresee. But contract law has never required foresight of every term: a person who signs a lengthy standard form without reading it is bound by provisions that surprise her.

There is also a practical argument. The counterparty to an automated transaction usually cannot see how the agent was configured or what limits its user intended to impose. The user, by contrast, chose the agent, set its parameters, and can monitor its conduct. If losses from an agent’s unexpected bargains must fall on someone, they should fall on the party best positioned to prevent them. A rule permitting users to disown inconvenient transactions would invite strategic repudiation and would make counterparties reluctant to deal with agents at all, sacrificing the efficiencies that make such agents valuable.

Passage B

Proposals to hold users strictly bound by whatever their software agents agree to rest on a misleading picture of how these agents work. A vending machine executes a fixed offer its owner composed in advance; the owner knows every transaction it can conclude. Contemporary agents, by contrast, generate terms their users never contemplated, sometimes by combining provisions in ways no one designed. To say that a user “assented” to such terms by deploying the agent stretches the notion of assent until it means nothing more than causation.

A better model already exists in the law of agency. A human agent binds the principal only when acting within the authority the principal conferred, or when the principal’s own conduct led the other party reasonably to believe such authority existed. Applied to software, this framework would bind users to transactions within the parameters they set—a spending ceiling, a list of approved vendors—and to transactions a counterparty reasonably believed were authorized, given the representations the user made about the agent. Transactions outside both categories would not bind the user.

This approach preserves the incentive that strict liability is meant to create: users who wish to be bound broadly can say so, and users who describe their agents carelessly will bear the consequences. But it also recognizes that some transactions are malfunctions rather than bargains, and that a counterparty who accepts terms no reasonable user would authorize—an order for ten thousand times the customary quantity, say—is not an innocent party deserving protection.
passages.subject: law

passages.title: The Tabrin Basin polygons
passages.text:
Across the floor of the Tabrin Basin, an arid lowland far from any present-day glacier, the ground is divided into a network of low ridges that outline polygons, most of them between fifteen and thirty meters across. Beneath each ridge lies a narrow, wedge-shaped body of sand that tapers downward to a depth of three or four meters. Two explanations for these features have been proposed, and the dispute between them has implications for the region’s climate history.

The first explanation holds that the polygons are giant desiccation cracks. When a layer of wet, clay-rich sediment dries, it shrinks, and the resulting stress is relieved by cracks that join into polygonal networks; windblown sand can then fill the cracks. The Tabrin Basin is known to have held a lake during wetter periods, and the drying of that lake would have left exactly the kind of clay layer in which such cracks form. Proponents note that desiccation polygons of considerable size have been documented on other dried lakebeds.

The second explanation holds that the polygons are relics of permafrost. In very cold climates, frozen ground contracts in winter and cracks; meltwater or windblown sediment enters the cracks, and over many centuries the repeated process builds vertical wedges that push the adjacent ground up into ridges. When the climate warms, any ice in the wedges melts and the space fills with sediment, leaving a “cast” of the former wedge. On this view, the Tabrin Basin was once far colder than any current reconstruction of its climate allows.

The size and depth of the features favor the second explanation. Desiccation cracks penetrate only about as deep as the drying layer, and the polygons they form are typically a few meters across at most; the large dried-lake examples are exceptional, and even they are bounded by cracks that rarely exceed a meter in depth. Wedges three meters deep would require a drying clay layer of comparable thickness, yet the clay deposits in the basin are nowhere more than half a meter thick. Moreover, much of the sand in the Tabrin wedges is arranged in thin vertical laminae, the pattern produced when sediment trickles repeatedly into a crack that reopens year after year—a hallmark of seasonal thermal contraction rather than of a single episode of drying. Proponents of the desiccation hypothesis have yet to explain these laminae. Admittedly, the permafrost explanation carries a cost its rival does not: it requires a cold interval for which no independent evidence has yet been found, and a hypothesis that demands revising a region’s climate record ought to meet a higher burden than one that does not. But a higher burden is not an insurmountable one, and unless the laminae can be otherwise explained, the basin’s polygons are best read as evidence of a cold interval that climate reconstructions have so far missed.
passages.subject: natural-science

passages.title: Why rotating savings associations persist
passages.text:
In many parts of the world, small groups of people pool their savings through rotating associations: each member contributes a fixed sum at every meeting, and the entire pot goes to one member in turn until everyone has received it once. For several decades, the prevailing interpretation among economists, associated most closely with the work of Hollis Brandt, treated these associations as a substitute for banking. Members, on this view, lack access to formal financial institutions and so improvise a crude mechanism for accumulating lump sums. The prediction followed naturally: as banks extend their reach, the associations should wither.

That prediction has fared poorly. In a survey of market vendors in the city of Merovale, conducted a decade after a national program brought bank branches to nearly every district, the anthropologist Ines Valdora found that more than half of the vendors who held bank accounts also belonged to at least one rotating association, and many contributed more to their associations than they deposited in their accounts. Nor could the persistence be attributed to mere habit: new associations were forming at roughly the same rate as before the branches opened. Nor did members appear to distrust banks: association members were no more likely than nonmembers to describe banks as unsafe, and almost none had closed an account.

Valdora’s interviews suggest why. Vendors repeatedly described the associations not as a way to obtain savings services they otherwise lacked but as a way to protect their savings from themselves and from others. Money in a bank account can be withdrawn whenever a relative asks for help or a tempting purchase appears; a contribution owed to the association at the next meeting cannot be postponed without public embarrassment. The association thus supplies something a bank account does not: an obligation, enforced by the regard of one’s neighbors, to keep saving. Some vendors added that a pot received from the association was easier to refuse to share than a bank balance, because it was understood to be earmarked for a purpose announced to the group in advance.

None of this implies that Brandt was simply wrong. Where banks were absent, the associations surely did serve as substitutes, and the earlier interpretation helps explain why they were once so widespread. Its error was to infer, from the circumstances in which the associations flourished, the full set of needs they meet. Valdora’s sample, drawn from the vendors of a single city, cannot by itself show that the same needs sustain associations elsewhere; it is enough, however, to show that the substitution account is incomplete. A practice adopted for one reason may persist for another, and only by observing what happens when the original reason disappears can the two be separated.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The English translation of The Salt Ledger introduced repetitions that critics mistakenly attributed to Malek’s declining powers.
Much of the repetition in The Salt Ledger that critics took as a sign of decline is better understood as a deliberate use of techniques from the oral tradition in which Malek was raised.
Every repetition in The Salt Ledger serves a structural purpose that critics overlooked because they read the novel in translation.
Oral storytellers on the Dravan coast valued artful variation on familiar material more highly than the invention of new stories.
The Salt Ledger should be judged by the standards of oral performance rather than those of the realist novel, since Malek intended it to be read aloud.
questions.explanation: The passage argues that the repetitions critics treated as lapses mostly follow the logic of the Dravan coast oral narratives, and (B)’s ‘much of’ matches the author’s concession that a few repetitions may be lapses. (C) is the main trap: it overstates both the scope, since the author grants that some sentences ‘seem to do no work at all,’ and the role of translation, since some reviewers of the original had the same complaint. (A) gets the translator’s effect backwards: the translator varied the repetitions rather than introducing them.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall point about the repetition in The Salt Ledger.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: End of paragraph 1 ("she was attempting something else entirely"), the concession at the end of paragraph 3, and the last sentence of the passage.

breakdown.analysis: Critics: the repetition is a sign of an aging writer losing control. Author: no, most of it is deliberate, drawn from the oral storytelling Malek grew up with. But the author hedges: a few repeated sentences "seem to do no work at all" and might be real lapses, and the translation isn't the whole story. Prephrase: much of the repetition is a deliberate oral-tradition technique, not decline. Lesson: the scope word matters; "much of" fits an author who conceded exceptions, "every" doesn't.

choices.note: Gets the translation backwards. The translator varied the wording of recurring passages, reducing exact repetition. The repetitions are Malek's.
CORRECT. "Much of" matches the concession that a few sentences may be lapses, and "deliberate use of techniques from the oral tradition" is the author's reading in P2-P3.

The main trap. "Every repetition" ignores the author's admission that some sentences "seem to do no work at all." And blaming translation alone ignores that "some reviewers who read the original voiced the same complaint."
A detail from P2 that supports the argument, not the main point. The passage is about the novel, not about ranking storytelling values.
The passage never says Malek intended the novel to be read aloud. The author says she borrowed oral techniques, not that it's meant for performance.

questions.stem: According to the passage, listeners to the communal narratives of the Dravan coast judged a performance primarily by
choices: how many of the familiar formulaic phrases the teller managed to include
the teller’s faithfulness to the traditional wording of the tale
how closely the teller’s version followed an outline the listeners already knew
how skillfully the teller varied material the listeners already knew
how much new material the teller could introduce without losing the audience
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says listeners ‘judged a performance by how artfully the teller varied the familiar,’ which is (D). (C) is the trap: the passage says listeners already knew the outline, but knowing the outline was the background to their judgment, not its standard. (B) is contradicted by the statement that the narratives ‘were never fixed texts.’

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find how Dravan coast listeners judged a storyteller's performance.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, third sentence: "listeners ... judged a performance by how artfully the teller varied the familiar."

breakdown.analysis: Detail question with a near-quote answer. Listeners already knew the outline; what they judged was how artfully the teller varied the familiar. Prephrase: skill at varying what they already knew. Like fans of a jazz standard who judge the soloist not on hitting the melody but on how they play with it.

choices.note: Counting formulas isn't the standard. The phrases are raw material; the judgment is about how they're varied.
Contradicted. The narratives "were never fixed texts," so there was no traditional wording to be faithful to.
The trap. Knowing the outline was the background, not the yardstick. Listeners judged the variation, not how closely the outline was followed.
CORRECT. Matches "judged a performance by how artfully the teller varied the familiar."
Wrong emphasis. The tradition prized variation on known material; "a small change in a phrase they knew by heart carried more weight than any new sentence could."

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that a reader of the English edition of The Salt Ledger who attended closely to every recurrence of the harbor passage would most likely
choices: have difficulty determining which of the differences between recurrences register the village’s losses
find that the recurrences differ from one another less than they do in the original
find the recurrences identical to one another, as many reviewers complained
be able to reconstruct Malek’s original wording from the pattern of the translator’s variations
conclude that Malek had chosen to narrate the village’s losses directly elsewhere in the novel
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says each recurrence of the harbor passage alters one detail that registers a loss. The fourth says the translator’s rewording buries Malek’s deliberate alterations ‘among many incidental ones.’ Together these support (A). (B) reverses the translator’s effect, since varying the wording makes the recurrences differ more, and (C) is wrong for the same reason. (E) contradicts the claim that Malek refuses to narrate these events directly.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Predict what a careful English-edition reader would experience reading each recurrence of the harbor passage.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3 (each harbor recurrence alters one detail that registers a loss) and paragraph 4 (translator's alterations are "lost among many incidental ones").

breakdown.analysis: Combine two facts. Malek's version: each harbor recurrence changes one meaningful detail. Translation: the translator reworded recurring passages, so lots of meaningless differences were added. A careful reader sees many differences and can't tell which ones matter. Prephrase: hard to pick out the meaningful changes. It's like finding the one changed word in a paragraph after someone rewrote half the sentences.

choices.note: CORRECT. The translator buried Malek's deliberate alterations among incidental ones, so a close reader of the English would struggle to tell which differences register the village's losses.
Reversed. Varying the wording makes the English recurrences differ more, not less.
Wrong for the same reason. The translator varied the wording, so the recurrences wouldn't be identical.
No basis. If Malek's changes are lost among the translator's, the pattern of variations wouldn't let you rebuild her wording.
Contradicts P3: Malek "deliberately refuses to narrate directly" these losses.

questions.stem: The author mentions the widow Anka primarily in order to
choices: show that Malek’s narrator states judgments of characters more openly than the critics recognized
demonstrate that the translator’s alterations did the most damage in the case of epithets
provide evidence that the novel’s repetitions are concentrated in its treatment of minor characters
suggest that the novel’s epithets, unlike its harbor passage, derive from Malek’s earlier realist practice
illustrate how a slight alteration to a recurring phrase can convey a judgment the narrative never makes explicit
questions.explanation: Adding ‘still’ to Anka’s fixed epithet ‘conveys a judgment the narrator never voices.’ The example therefore shows the technique described in (E). (A) is the trap: it borrows the passage’s language about judgment but reverses the relationship, since the point is that the narrator does not state the judgment. Nothing supports (B), (C), or (D).

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain why the author brings up the widow Anka.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3: "The epithets work similarly..." and the Anka sentence.

breakdown.analysis: The harbor passage showed a small change carrying meaning. "The epithets work similarly": Anka is always "the patient one," and then "the patient one, still." One word adds a judgment the narrator never says outright. Prephrase: an example of a tiny change to a repeated phrase conveying an unstated judgment. Lesson: when a passage says "work similarly," the example illustrates the technique just described.

choices.note: The trap. Uses the word "judgment" but flips it: the point is that the narrator never voices it. It's conveyed indirectly, not stated openly.
The Anka example isn't about the translation at all, and the passage never says epithets suffered most.
Nothing says repetitions cluster around minor characters. The harbor passage, a main example, isn't about a character.
Opposite. "The epithets work similarly" to the harbor passage, both drawn from the oral tradition, not from her realist past.
CORRECT. Adding "still" to a fixed epithet "conveys a judgment the narrator never voices." That's exactly what E describes.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the author’s position regarding the claim that the repetitions in The Salt Ledger are lapses?
choices: The author rejects the claim categorically, holding that every repetition in the novel can be traced to the oral tradition.
The author accepts the claim as applied to the English edition but rejects it as applied to the original.
The author rejects the claim as an account of the novel’s repetition in general, while allowing that it may hold for a few recurring sentences.
The author regards the claim as plausible but finds that the critics who advanced it offered too little evidence for it.
The author considers the claim correct as to the middle chapters but irrelevant to an evaluation of the novel as a whole.
questions.explanation: The author offers an alternative account of the repetitions but concedes that a few unaltered sentences may be ‘the lapses the critics took the whole book to be.’ That partial rejection is (C). (E) is the closest trap, but it overstates the concession: the author says only that it is ‘possible’ those sentences are lapses, not that the claim is correct for them, and never calls the claim irrelevant. (A) ignores the concession, and (B) misreads the translation discussion.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe the author's stance on the critics' claim that the repetitions are lapses.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, last three sentences ("Not every repetition yields to this reading...").

breakdown.analysis: The author mostly rejects the critics: the repetitions have a pattern and a purpose. But concedes: a few unaltered middle-chapter sentences "seem to do no work at all," and "it is possible" those are real lapses. Then: an interpretation needn't redeem every sentence. Prephrase: rejects it overall, allows it may apply to a few sentences. Lesson: attitude answers have to keep the concession and its exact strength ("possible," not "correct").

choices.note: Ignores the concession. The author doesn't say every repetition traces to the oral tradition; some "seem to do no work at all."
Misreads P4. The translation hid Malek's pattern; that doesn't make the lapse claim true of the English edition. And some reviewers of the original made the same complaint.
CORRECT. Rejects the lapse claim for the novel's repetition generally, but allows a few unaltered sentences may be "the lapses the critics took the whole book to be."
The author doesn't find the claim plausible overall; the author offers a better reading. The issue isn't the critics' lack of evidence.
Closest trap, but too strong both ways. The author says only that it's "possible" those sentences are lapses, not that the claim is correct there. And the author never calls the claim irrelevant.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most analogous to the function that the passage attributes to recurring phrases in helping Dravan coast audiences keep track of where they were in a performance?
choices: a footnote in a scholarly book that identifies the source of a quotation
a refrain in a long ballad that lets listeners recognize which part of the song has been reached
a summary on a book’s cover that tells prospective readers what the story concerns
a recurring melody in a film score that is varied slightly to show that a character has changed
a revised edition of a textbook that corrects errors in an earlier edition
questions.explanation: The stem asks about orientation: a recurring phrase ‘signaled to the audience where they stood in the tale.’ A ballad refrain that marks progress through the song does the same, as in (B). (D) is the trap: it is analogous to the other function the passage mentions, in which a small change to a known phrase carries meaning, but that is not the orienting function the stem asks about. (C) orients the reader only once, before the work begins.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the example that does what recurring phrases did for Dravan coast audiences: tell them where they were in the story.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, last sentence: "a recurring phrase signaled to the audience where they stood in the tale."

breakdown.analysis: Paragraph 2 gives two functions of repetition: (1) orientation, a familiar phrase tells you where you are; (2) meaning through small variation. The stem asks only about (1). Prephrase: something that repeats through a long work so you know which part you've reached. Lesson: when a passage names two functions, read the stem for which one it wants.

choices.note: A footnote gives a source. It doesn't repeat or tell you where you are in the work.
CORRECT. A refrain recurs throughout a long ballad and lets listeners recognize which part of the song they've reached. That's the orienting function.
A cover summary happens once, before the work starts. It doesn't recur to mark your place.
The trap. A slightly varied melody showing change matches the other function (small change to a known phrase carrying meaning). The stem asks about keeping track of position.
A revised edition corrects errors. Nothing about repetition orienting an audience.

questions.stem: The author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements about the English translation of The Salt Ledger?
choices: It was responsible for the unfavorable verdict of those reviewers who did not read the original.
It eliminated the deliberate alterations that Malek made to her recurring passages.
It made the novel appear more repetitive than the original actually is.
It made it harder for readers to tell Malek’s intentional variations from incidental ones.
It was produced by a translator unfamiliar with the oral traditions of the Dravan coast.
questions.explanation: The translator’s rewording means that Malek’s alterations ‘are lost among many incidental ones,’ so readers of the translation would struggle to tell which changes were deliberate, which is (D). (B) is the trap: ‘lost among’ means hidden, not removed. (A) overstates what the author claims, since some reviewers of the original voiced the same complaint, and (C) reverses the translator’s effect of reducing repetition.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the statement about the English translation that the author would agree with.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4.

breakdown.analysis: P4: the translator varied recurring passages to avoid monotony, so Malek's deliberate alterations "are lost among many incidental ones." The author also says the critics' verdict wasn't produced entirely by the translation. Prephrase: the translation made it hard to spot Malek's meaningful changes. Lesson: "lost among" means hidden in a crowd, not deleted.

choices.note: Too strong. The author says it would be "too much to say" the verdict was produced entirely by the translation; some reviewers of the original said the same. The author claims only that English readers had "little chance" to see the pattern.
The trap. "Lost among many incidental ones" means buried, not removed. Malek's alterations are still in there, just hard to see.
Reversed. The translator varied the wording "to avoid monotony," making it look less repetitive, not more.
CORRECT. With the translator's incidental changes mixed in, readers can't easily tell Malek's deliberate variations from the translator's.
Unsupported. The passage says the translator treated the repetitions as lapses, not that they were unfamiliar with Dravan traditions. Possible, but the author never says it.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of passage B?
choices: Rather than binding users to every transaction their software agents conclude, the law should bind them only to transactions within the agents’ actual or reasonably apparent authority.
Software agents are too unpredictable to be used for concluding contracts unless a human reviews the terms of each transaction.
Users of software agents should never be held responsible for contract terms that they did not personally contemplate.
Transactions concluded by software agents should bind users only when those transactions fall within parameters the users themselves specified.
Counterparties who deal with software agents should bear all of the losses that result from agent malfunctions.
questions.explanation: Passage B rejects strict binding and proposes the agency-law test of conferred or reasonably apparent authority, which is (A). (D) is the trap: it captures only the first of passage B’s two categories and leaves out transactions that a counterparty reasonably believed were authorized. (C) is too strong for the same reason.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the main point of passage B only.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, first sentence (rejecting strict binding) and second paragraph (the agency-law rule and its two categories).

breakdown.analysis: Passage B: binding users to everything their agents agree to rests on a bad picture of how agents work. Better rule from agency law: users are bound (1) within the parameters they set, and (2) where a counterparty reasonably believed the transaction was authorized. Outside both, not bound. Prephrase: bind users only within actual or apparent authority. Lesson: when a rule has two parts, an answer with only one part is incomplete.

choices.note: CORRECT. Rejects binding users to every transaction and adopts the agency-law test: actual authority (parameters set) or reasonably apparent authority (what the counterparty reasonably believed).
B never says human review is required. B's rule works through parameters and representations, not checking each deal.
Too strong. Users are bound by uncontemplated terms if those terms fall within the parameters set or reasonably appeared authorized.
The trap. It has only the first category. It drops transactions the counterparty reasonably believed were authorized, which B also says bind the user.
Too strong. B says only that a counterparty who accepts terms no reasonable user would authorize isn't an innocent party. Losses within apparent authority still fall on the user.

questions.stem: Both passages are primarily concerned with answering which one of the following questions?
choices: Should users be required to review the terms of transactions their software agents conclude?
Is the law of agency the appropriate source of rules governing automated transactions?
Under what circumstances should users be bound by transactions their software agents conclude?
What representations should users make to counterparties about the capabilities of their agents?
Should the law of agency be replaced by a new body of law governing automated transactions?
questions.explanation: Passage A answers that users should be bound in nearly every case, and passage B answers that they should be bound only within actual or apparent authority, so both address (C). (B) is the trap: agency law is central to passage B but never mentioned in passage A. (D) also concerns only passage B, and neither passage proposes the review requirement in (A).

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the question both passages are trying to answer.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, end of the first paragraph ("The answer should be yes, in nearly every case"); passage B, second paragraph's rule.

breakdown.analysis: Passage A: users should be bound in nearly every case. Passage B: users should be bound only within actual or apparent authority. Same question, different answers: when is a user bound by what their agent agreed to? Lesson: a shared-question answer has to fit both passages; something central to only one is a trap.

choices.note: Neither passage proposes requiring review. Passage A notes agents act "often without any human reviewing the particular terms" as a fact, not a debated rule.
The trap. Agency law is central to passage B, but passage A never mentions it.
CORRECT. A says "nearly every case"; B says "only within authority conferred or reasonably apparent." Both are answering when users are bound.
Only passage B talks about users' representations, and even there it's a piece of the rule, not the main question.
Backwards for B, which wants to apply agency law, not replace it. And A doesn't mention agency law.

questions.stem: According to passage A, a rule permitting users to disown transactions concluded by their software agents would
choices: require courts to examine how each agent was configured
place losses on the party best positioned to prevent them
be inconsistent with the traditional requirement of mutual assent
encourage users to configure their agents with less care
make counterparties reluctant to transact with software agents
questions.explanation: Passage A states that such a rule ‘would make counterparties reluctant to deal with agents at all,’ which is (E). (D) is the trap: passage A says the rule would ‘invite strategic repudiation,’ which concerns disowning transactions after the fact, not careless configuration. (B) reverses the passage’s point, and (C) is never claimed; passage A argues only that its own rule is consistent with mutual assent.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what passage A says would happen under a rule letting users disown their agents' deals.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, last sentence of the third paragraph.

breakdown.analysis: Passage A gives two consequences: it would "invite strategic repudiation" and "make counterparties reluctant to deal with agents at all." The answer will be one of these. Prephrase: counterparties would avoid agents. Lesson: "strategic repudiation" means backing out of deals you regret, not being sloppy up front.

choices.note: Passage A doesn't say this. It mentions counterparties can't see configurations, but never says such a rule would make courts examine them.
Reversed. Passage A says losses should fall on the party best positioned to prevent them, the user. A disown rule would shift losses away from the user.
Never claimed. A argues its own rule is consistent with mutual assent; it doesn't say the opposing rule violates it.
The trap. A says the rule would "invite strategic repudiation": backing out of deals afterward. That's not the same as configuring agents carelessly.
CORRECT. Passage A: such a rule "would make counterparties reluctant to deal with agents at all."

questions.stem: The author of passage B would be most likely to respond to the vending-machine analogy in passage A by pointing out that
choices: a vending machine’s owner, unlike a software agent’s user, has an opportunity to approve each sale before it occurs
the analogy holds only if the deploying party fixed in advance the range of transactions that could result, which contemporary agents do not allow
vending-machine owners are generally not bound by sales made while their machines are malfunctioning
general assent, though recognized for vending machines, has never been recognized in the law governing human agents
the analogy, properly understood, shows that the user rather than the counterparty is best positioned to prevent losses
questions.explanation: Passage B distinguishes a vending machine, which ‘executes a fixed offer its owner composed in advance,’ from agents that ‘generate terms their users never contemplated.’ That disanalogy is (B). (C) is attractive because passage B discusses malfunctions, but it makes no claim about how the law treats malfunctioning machines. (A) contradicts passage A’s accurate premise that the owner need not approve each sale, and (E) argues for passage A’s side.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Predict how passage B's author would answer passage A's vending-machine analogy.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, second paragraph (the analogy); passage B, first paragraph ("A vending machine executes a fixed offer...").

breakdown.analysis: Passage A: deploying an agent is like installing a vending machine; you assent generally to whatever sales happen. Passage B: a vending machine sells a fixed offer composed in advance; the owner knows every possible transaction. Modern agents invent terms no one contemplated. Prephrase: the analogy breaks because vending-machine owners fixed the possible deals in advance and agent users don't. Lesson: the best rebuttal to an analogy names the relevant difference.

choices.note: Contradicts passage A's premise, which B doesn't dispute: no one thinks the vending-machine owner must approve each sale. B's point is about advance knowledge, not approval.

CORRECT. B: the machine "executes a fixed offer its owner composed in advance," while agents "generate terms their users never contemplated." The analogy needs the range fixed in advance, which agents don't provide.
Tempting since B discusses malfunctions, but B says nothing about how the law treats malfunctioning vending machines. Unsupported.
B never says general assent is unknown in agency law. B's point is about what the user can foresee, not about the history of general assent.
That helps passage A, not B. "Best positioned to prevent losses" is A's practical argument.

questions.stem: The author of passage A mentions that the counterparty to an automated transaction ‘usually cannot see how the agent was configured’ primarily in order to
choices: rebut the objection that users cannot assent to terms they did not foresee
explain why counterparties are already reluctant to deal with software agents
show that mutual assent is absent from most automated transactions
support the claim that losses from an agent’s unexpected bargains should fall on its user
suggest that users should be required to disclose the parameters of their agents
questions.explanation: The remark sets up a contrast with the user, who ‘chose the agent, set its parameters, and can monitor its conduct,’ and supports the conclusion that losses belong with the party best positioned to prevent them, the user. That is (D). (A) is the trap: passage A does rebut that objection, but in the previous paragraph and with the standard-form analogy, not with this remark. (E) is a policy passage A never proposes, and (B) treats a predicted consequence of a different rule as a present fact.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain why passage A says the counterparty usually can't see how the agent was configured.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage A, third paragraph (the practical argument).

breakdown.analysis: The paragraph sets up a contrast: counterparty can't see the configuration; user chose the agent, set parameters, can monitor it. Then the conclusion: losses should fall on whoever is best positioned to prevent them. So the remark supports putting losses on the user. Prephrase: to show the user, not the counterparty, should bear the losses. Lesson: half of a contrast supports the conclusion the contrast leads to.

choices.note: The trap. A does rebut that objection, but in the previous paragraph, with the unread-standard-form analogy. This remark is part of the separate practical argument.
Counterparty reluctance is a predicted result of a different rule (letting users disown deals), not a current fact this remark explains.
Opposite of A's view. A argues mutual assent is present (general assent).
CORRECT. The counterparty's blindness, contrasted with the user's control, supports the conclusion that losses should fall on "the party best positioned to prevent them," the user.
A never proposes a disclosure requirement. That's closer to passage B's interest in users' representations.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between passage A and passage B?
choices: Passage B rejects the conception of assent on which passage A partly relies and offers a rule meant to secure the incentive passage A values while sparing users some losses passage A would impose.
Passage B rejects passage A’s account of assent but accepts its conclusion that users should be bound by nearly all of their agents’ transactions.
Passage B argues that the transactions on which passage A’s argument depends occur far less often than passage A assumes.
Passage A defends a rule on grounds of efficiency, and passage B argues that efficiency is an inappropriate basis for contract doctrine.
Passage B agrees with passage A that users should bear losses from agent malfunctions but disputes the reasoning passage A offers for that view.
questions.explanation: Passage B says passage A’s notion of assent collapses into ‘causation.’ It then proposes an agency-law rule that ‘preserves the incentive that strict liability is meant to create’ while freeing users from malfunctions outside their actual or apparent authority. That is (A). (D) is the strongest trap: passage B does depart from passage A’s efficiency-driven rule, but it explicitly keeps the incentive rationale rather than rejecting efficiency as a basis. (B) and (E) misstate passage B’s conclusion, since passage B would not bind users to malfunctions outside those categories.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how passage B relates to passage A.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Passage B, first paragraph (assent "means nothing more than causation") and third paragraph ("preserves the incentive that strict liability is meant to create").

breakdown.analysis: B does two things to A. It attacks A's assent argument: deploying an agent isn't real assent, just causation. And it keeps something A cares about: users still have an incentive to describe agents carefully. But B frees users from obvious malfunctions outside their authority, losses A would make them bear. Prephrase: rejects A's assent theory, offers a rule that keeps A's incentive but spares users some losses. Lesson: on relationship questions, check for both disagreement and partial agreement.

choices.note: CORRECT. B rejects the general-assent conception ("stretches the notion of assent until it means nothing more than causation"), and offers a rule that "preserves the incentive" while not binding users to transactions outside actual or apparent authority.
B doesn't accept A's conclusion. B would not bind users to transactions outside both authority categories, so it's not "nearly all."
B never argues about how often such transactions happen. It argues about what rule should govern them.
Strongest trap. B departs from A's rule, but it explicitly keeps the incentive rationale. B never says efficiency is an inappropriate basis.
Opposite. B says some transactions are "malfunctions rather than bargains" and the user isn't bound by those outside authority. B doesn't agree users should bear those losses.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The Tabrin features provide conclusive evidence of a cold interval in the basin’s history that climate reconstructions have missed.
Because desiccation and thermal contraction both produce polygonal networks, the origin of the Tabrin features cannot yet be determined.
The dimensions and internal structure of the Tabrin features favor a permafrost origin, despite the higher burden that explanation must meet.
Climate reconstructions of the Tabrin Basin are unreliable because they fail to account for the lake that once occupied it.
The desiccation hypothesis fails because the Tabrin Basin did not contain enough clay to produce polygons of the observed size.
questions.explanation: The final paragraph argues from size, depth, and laminae that the permafrost origin is better supported, while conceding that this explanation must meet a higher burden. (C) captures both. (A) is the trap: the author says the polygons are ‘best read’ as such evidence ‘unless the laminae can be otherwise explained,’ which is not conclusive. (E) misplaces the problem: the issue is the depth of the clay, not the size of the polygons, and the depth argument is only part of the case.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall conclusion about where the Tabrin polygons came from.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4: first sentence ("favor the second explanation") and the last two sentences (the higher-burden concession and "best read as evidence").

breakdown.analysis: P2 and P3 lay out two explanations. P4 is the author's verdict: size, depth, and the laminae favor permafrost. The author admits permafrost must meet a higher bar because it rewrites the climate record, but says the bar can be met. Prephrase: the evidence favors permafrost, despite its higher burden. Lesson: "best read as ... unless" is a strong lean, not proof; don't pick "conclusive."

choices.note: The trap. Right direction, wrong strength. The author says "best read as" such evidence "unless the laminae can be otherwise explained." That's not conclusive.
The author does pick a side. And the passage says the features differ in depth and laminae, not that both processes fit equally.
CORRECT. Dimensions (size, depth) and internal structure (laminae) favor permafrost, and the author concedes the higher burden. Both halves are in P4.
The author never calls reconstructions unreliable for ignoring the lake. The lake is part of the desiccation hypothesis; the author says reconstructions may have missed a cold interval.
Misplaces the problem and too narrow. The clay issue is its thickness relative to wedge depth, not polygon size. And the laminae are a separate, key part of the case.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the clay deposits in the Tabrin Basin
choices: were laid down during an interval when the ground was permanently frozen
contain thin vertical laminae of windblown sand
are thicker beneath the ridges than at the centers of the polygons
extend to a depth of three or four meters in places
are no more than half a meter thick anywhere in the basin
questions.explanation: The fourth paragraph says the clay deposits ‘are nowhere more than half a meter thick,’ which is (E). (D) is the trap: three or four meters is the depth of the sand wedges, not of the clay. (B) also attributes a feature of the wedges to the clay.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the passage says about the basin's clay deposits.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, the sentence "yet the clay deposits in the basin are nowhere more than half a meter thick."

breakdown.analysis: Detail question. Keep the two materials apart: clay is the thin layer left by the lake (half a meter max); sand fills the wedges (three to four meters deep, with laminae). Prephrase: half a meter or less, everywhere. Lesson: detail traps love to swap a number or feature from one thing onto a neighbor.

choices.note: The clay came from the drying lake (a wet period), not from frozen ground. The passage never links the clay to permafrost.
The laminae are in the sand wedges, not the clay.
Nothing compares clay thickness under ridges vs. polygon centers.
The trap. Three or four meters is the depth of the sand wedges. The clay is no more than half a meter thick.
CORRECT. The clay deposits "are nowhere more than half a meter thick."

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that, in order to answer the author’s objections, proponents of the desiccation hypothesis would most need to establish that
choices: the Tabrin Basin held a lake during at least one wetter period of its history
cracks produced by drying can extend several meters below a thin clay layer and reopen repeatedly
desiccation polygons on some other dried lakebeds are more than fifteen meters across
independent evidence of a cold interval in the region’s history is unlikely ever to be found
windblown sand was abundant in the basin at the time the lake dried
questions.explanation: The author objects that the wedges are far deeper than the thin clay layer allows and that their laminae indicate repeated reopening, and (B) answers both. (C) is the main trap: the author already grants that large desiccation polygons exist, so width is not in dispute. The objection concerns depth and lamination. (D) would at most bear on the permafrost explanation’s burden; it would do nothing to explain the depth or the laminae, which the author says must be explained.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Figure out what desiccation supporters would need to show to answer the author's objections.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4: the depth objection (cracks only as deep as the drying layer; clay is half a meter) and the laminae objection (repeated reopening).

breakdown.analysis: List the objections, then find the answer that meets them. Objection 1: drying cracks only go as deep as the drying layer, and the clay is thin, but the wedges are 3-4 meters deep. Objection 2: vertical laminae show a crack reopening year after year, not one drying event. Prephrase: drying cracks can go meters below thin clay and reopen repeatedly. Lesson: to rescue a theory, answer the objections actually raised, not ones already conceded.

choices.note: Already accepted. The basin "is known to have held a lake." The author's objections don't dispute this.
CORRECT. This answers both objections at once: deep cracks below a thin clay layer (depth) and repeated reopening (laminae).
The main trap. The author already grants that large desiccation polygons exist on other lakebeds. Width isn't the problem; depth and laminae are.
At most this bears on the permafrost side's burden. It doesn't explain the depth or the laminae, which the author says must be explained.
Sand supply isn't questioned. The author's problem is how the cracks got so deep and why they kept reopening.

questions.stem: The author mentions that large desiccation polygons on other dried lakebeds ‘are bounded by cracks that rarely exceed a meter in depth’ primarily in order to
choices: counter a possible objection based on evidence that proponents of the desiccation hypothesis have cited
concede that drying can produce polygons as large as those in the Tabrin Basin
suggest that the other dried lakebeds were once underlain by permafrost
explain why the sand in the Tabrin wedges is arranged in vertical laminae
establish that the lake that once occupied the Tabrin Basin was unusually shallow
questions.explanation: Proponents cite large desiccation polygons on other lakebeds. The author replies that even those have shallow cracks, so they do not match the three-meter Tabrin wedges. That is (A). (B) is the trap: the clause does acknowledge that such polygons exist, but its purpose is to neutralize the proponents’ evidence, not to concede a point. The concession appears earlier in the same sentence, in ‘the large dried-lake examples are exceptional.’

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain why the author says large desiccation polygons elsewhere have cracks that "rarely exceed a meter in depth."

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, last sentence (proponents cite large lakebed polygons); paragraph 4, second sentence.

breakdown.analysis: In P2, desiccation supporters point to big drying polygons on other lakebeds. The author anticipates that: fine, those are big, but their cracks are only about a meter deep, far short of the Tabrin wedges' three meters. So the remark takes the proponents' evidence and shows it doesn't match. Prephrase: to neutralize the proponents' lakebed evidence. It's like answering "other kids got As in that class too" with "yes, but none of them skipped the final."

choices.note: CORRECT. Proponents cite large lakebed polygons; the author replies that even those have shallow cracks, so they don't match the deep Tabrin wedges. That counters an objection based on the proponents' own evidence.
The trap. The sentence does acknowledge big polygons exist ("exceptional"), but the depth clause is there to take that evidence away, not to give ground.
No suggestion of permafrost under other lakebeds. They're described as desiccation polygons.
The laminae come up later in the paragraph, as a separate point. Shallow cracks elsewhere don't explain them.
Nothing about the lake's depth. The issue is the clay layer's thickness and the cracks' depth.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken the author’s argument for the permafrost explanation?
choices: Polygons formed by ice wedges in present-day cold regions are commonly between ten and forty meters across and are outlined by low ridges.
The laminae in the Tabrin wedges are somewhat thinner and less regular than those typically found in sand wedges in present-day permafrost.
Climate reconstructions for the Tabrin Basin rest largely on pollen records, which are sparse for several long intervals of the basin’s history.
Where clay is repeatedly rewetted by rising groundwater, drying cracks have been observed to reopen along the same lines each season and to deepen well below the clay.
Large desiccation polygons have been documented on several more dried lakebeds since the desiccation hypothesis was first proposed.
questions.explanation: The author’s case rests on two claims: drying cannot crack deeper than the thin clay layer, and laminae require seasonal thermal contraction. (D) describes a non-freezing process that produces deep cracks reopening every season, which undercuts both claims at once, and the basin is known to have been wet. (B) is the most tempting trap, but a modest difference from typical permafrost laminae provides no alternative mechanism and leaves the depth argument untouched. (E) adds evidence about polygon width, which the author already concedes. (A) and (C) strengthen the argument.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the fact that most weakens the author's case for permafrost.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4: the depth argument and the laminae argument.

breakdown.analysis: The author's case rests on two claims: (1) drying cracks can't go deeper than the thin clay, and (2) laminae mean a crack reopening every season, which only freezing produces. Best weakener: a non-freezing process that makes deep cracks that reopen every season. That kills both legs, and the basin was known to be wet. Prephrase: drying cracks can reopen yearly and go deep. Lesson: hit the premise the argument actually rests on, ideally both at once.

choices.note: Strengthens. Modern ice-wedge polygons matching the Tabrin size range and ridges makes the permafrost reading more plausible.
Most tempting trap. A small difference from typical permafrost laminae is a minor wrinkle; it offers no alternative mechanism and leaves the depth argument untouched.
Strengthens if anything. Sparse pollen records make it easier to believe reconstructions missed a cold interval.
CORRECT. Rising groundwater rewetting clay produces drying cracks that reopen along the same lines each season and go well below the clay. That explains deep wedges and laminae without any freezing.
More big desiccation polygons doesn't help. The author already concedes width; the problem is depth and laminae.

questions.stem: If the author’s explanation of the Tabrin features is correct, which one of the following can most reasonably be inferred about the sand that fills the wedges?
choices: All of it was deposited after the climate of the basin had warmed.
Most of it was derived from the clay deposits left by the former lake.
Some of it was deposited during the period in which the ground was repeatedly cracking.
It was deposited in a single episode following the melting of the wedges’ ice.
It accumulated more rapidly once the lake had dried than while the ground was frozen.
questions.explanation: The author reads the vertical laminae as sediment that entered ‘a crack that reopens year after year.’ On the author’s view, then, at least some sand arrived while seasonal cracking was still going on, which is (C). (A) and (D) are the traps. They come from the third paragraph’s account of a cast filling after warming, but they conflict with the laminae evidence the author relies on in the fourth paragraph. (E) mixes elements of the two rival explanations.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Assume the author is right (permafrost) and figure out what must be true of the sand in the wedges.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4: laminae as sediment that "trickles repeatedly into a crack that reopens year after year." Paragraph 3: the cast filling after warming.

breakdown.analysis: The author's key evidence is the laminae, which the author reads as sand trickling in each year while the crack kept reopening. So under the author's view, at least some of the sand went in during the cracking period. P3 also says sediment can fill the space after the ice melts, so not all of it has to be early. Prephrase: some sand was deposited while the ground was still cracking. Lesson: "some" is often the safest inference when the passage supports more than one timing.

choices.note: Trap. P3 says the space left by melted ice fills with sediment, but the author's laminae evidence needs sand entering during the cracking years. "All" after warming contradicts that.
No support. The sand is described as windblown or trickling in; the author's view doesn't need the lake's clay at all.
CORRECT. The author reads the laminae as sediment that entered "a crack that reopens year after year," so at least some sand went in during the cracking period.
Trap. A single episode is exactly what the laminae argue against; the author contrasts repeated reopening with "a single episode."
Mixes the two hypotheses. Under the author's view there's no lake-drying stage driving the wedges, and nothing compares rates.

questions.stem: The author’s attitude toward the permafrost explanation can most accurately be described as
choices: confident that the dimensions of the wedges establish it beyond reasonable doubt
tentatively favorable, but unwilling to accept it until the laminae have been explained
skeptical of it, because no independent evidence of a cold interval has been found
convinced that it is correct for the deepest wedges but not for the basin as a whole
persuaded that it is better supported than its rival, while acknowledging that it must meet a heavier burden
questions.explanation: The author says the evidence ‘favor[s]’ the permafrost explanation, concedes that it ‘ought to meet a higher burden,’ and holds that the burden ‘is not an insurmountable one.’ That is (E). (B) is the strongest trap: it reverses the role of the laminae, which are evidence for the permafrost view, not a puzzle it must solve. It is the desiccation hypothesis that has ‘yet to explain these laminae.’ (C) turns a conceded cost into a reason for skepticism that the author explicitly rejects, and (A) ignores the conditional ‘unless the laminae can be otherwise explained.’

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how the author feels about the permafrost explanation.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4: "favor the second explanation," "Proponents of the desiccation hypothesis have yet to explain these laminae," and the higher-burden concession.

breakdown.analysis: The author leans clearly toward permafrost ("favor," "best read as"), admits it must meet a higher burden, and says that burden "is not an insurmountable one." Prephrase: persuaded it's better supported, while admitting the higher bar. Lesson: keep track of whose problem a piece of evidence is; here the laminae are a problem for the rival theory, not for the author's.

choices.note: Too strong. The conclusion is conditional: "unless the laminae can be otherwise explained." That's not beyond reasonable doubt.
Strongest trap. It flips the laminae's role. They're evidence for permafrost; it's the desiccation side that has "yet to explain these laminae."
The author concedes the missing cold-interval evidence as a cost, then says the higher burden "is not an insurmountable one." That's not skepticism.
The author makes no split between deep wedges and the rest. The conclusion covers "the basin's polygons."
CORRECT. The evidence "favor[s]" permafrost, the author concedes it "ought to meet a higher burden," and says that burden can be met.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?
choices: The persistence of rotating savings associations after banks became available shows that they meet needs beyond substituting for banking, though the earlier view correctly identified one of their functions.
The earlier interpretation of rotating savings associations was mistaken in claiming that the associations ever functioned as substitutes for banks.
Rotating savings associations everywhere serve chiefly as devices for protecting savings rather than as substitutes for banks.
The persistence of associations in Merovale shows that their role as substitutes for banking was overstated even before banks were available.
The expansion of banking in Merovale changed the purposes for which vendors join rotating savings associations.
questions.explanation: The passage uses Valdora’s findings to show that the substitution account is incomplete, and it grants that the associations did serve as substitutes where banks were absent. That is (A). (C) is the strongest trap: it overgeneralizes, since the author says the single-city sample ‘cannot by itself show that the same needs sustain associations elsewhere.’ (D) contradicts the concession that the associations ‘surely did serve as substitutes,’ and (E) says banking created new purposes, which the passage never claims.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the author's overall point about rotating savings associations.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4: "None of this implies that Brandt was simply wrong," "the substitution account is incomplete," and the last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Brandt: associations substitute for banks, so they'll fade when banks arrive. Valdora: banks arrived and associations didn't fade, because they help people protect savings from themselves and others. Author: Brandt wasn't wrong, just incomplete; associations meet other needs too. And the author admits one city can't show this holds everywhere. Prephrase: persistence shows associations do more than substitute for banks, though Brandt got one function right. Lesson: when the author hedges scope ("a single city"), an answer with "everywhere" is out.

choices.note: CORRECT. Persistence after banks arrived shows needs beyond substitution ("the substitution account is incomplete"), and the earlier view correctly identified one function ("surely did serve as substitutes").
Opposite of the concession. The author says where banks were absent, the associations "surely did serve as substitutes."
Strongest trap. "Everywhere" overreaches; the author says one city's sample "cannot by itself show that the same needs sustain associations elsewhere."
Contradicts the concession. The author doesn't say the substitution role was overstated before banks came; it says that role was real.
The passage never says banking created new purposes. The author's point is that the other purposes were hidden until the substitution reason went away.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Valdora found that in Merovale
choices: association members were more likely than nonmembers to describe banks as unsafe
vendors with bank accounts contributed less to associations than they had before the branches opened
the number of rotating associations declined gradually after bank branches opened
new associations continued to form at about the same rate as before the branches opened
vendors preferred bank accounts for savings that were earmarked for a particular purpose
questions.explanation: The second paragraph states that ‘new associations were forming at roughly the same rate as before the branches opened,’ which is (D). (A) reverses the finding that members were ‘no more likely than nonmembers’ to call banks unsafe. (E) reverses the point that earmarked association pots were easier to protect than bank balances.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what Valdora found in Merovale.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2.

breakdown.analysis: Valdora's findings in P2: more than half of account-holding vendors also belonged to an association; many put more into associations than banks; new associations formed at about the same rate as before; members didn't distrust banks more than nonmembers. Prephrase: look for one of those. Lesson: detail traps often flip a comparison ("no more likely" becomes "more likely").

choices.note: Reversed. Members were "no more likely than nonmembers" to call banks unsafe.
Not reported. The passage compares contributions with deposits, not with contributions before the branches opened.
Contradicted. New associations kept forming at roughly the same rate; nothing says the number declined.
CORRECT. "New associations were forming at roughly the same rate as before the branches opened."
Reversed. Vendors said earmarked association pots were easier to protect than bank balances.

questions.stem: It can be inferred from the passage that the vendors Valdora interviewed would be most likely to regard which one of the following as a disadvantage of a bank account relative to a rotating association?
choices: Money held in a bank account is at greater risk of being lost through the failure of the institution.
Money in a bank account is harder to withhold from relatives who ask for help.
A bank account does not allow a saver to receive a lump sum before having saved the full amount.
Bank branches are located too far from the markets where the vendors work.
A bank account requires a minimum balance that many vendors cannot maintain.
questions.explanation: The vendors said bank money ‘can be withdrawn whenever a relative asks for help’ and that association pots were ‘easier to refuse to share,’ which supports (B). (C) is the most tempting trap because it describes a real feature of rotating associations, but the passage never mentions it, and the vendors stress protecting savings, not getting money early. (A) is ruled out by the finding that members were no more likely than nonmembers to call banks unsafe, and (D) is ruled out by the branches reaching ‘nearly every district.’

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what the interviewed vendors would see as a downside of a bank account compared with an association.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3 (what vendors said) and paragraph 2 (what they didn't think about banks).

breakdown.analysis: The vendors' theme: associations protect savings from themselves and from others. Bank money "can be withdrawn whenever a relative asks for help," while an association pot is "easier to refuse to share." Prephrase: bank money is easier for relatives to get at. It's like keeping cash in a jar on the counter vs. in a locked box your neighbors know about.

choices.note: Ruled out. Members were no more likely than nonmembers to call banks unsafe, and almost none closed accounts.
CORRECT. Vendors said bank money can be withdrawn "whenever a relative asks for help" and association pots were "easier to refuse to share."
Most tempting trap. Getting a lump sum early is a real feature of rotating associations, but the passage never mentions it, and the vendors focus on protecting savings, not getting money sooner.
Ruled out. Bank branches reached "nearly every district."
Minimum balances are never mentioned. Outside information.

questions.stem: The author mentions that new associations were forming at roughly the same rate as before the bank branches opened primarily in order to
choices: show that the national banking program failed to reach many vendors
suggest that the associations have become more popular since the banks arrived
establish that association members do not distrust banks
explain why vendors contribute more to associations than to bank accounts
rule out one alternative explanation for the persistence of the associations
questions.explanation: The sentence opens ‘Nor could the persistence be attributed to mere habit,’ and new associations forming shows active choice, not inertia. That is (E). (C) is the trap: ruling out distrust is the job of the next sentence, which cites different evidence. (B) overstates the point, since a steady rate shows continued demand, not growing popularity.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Explain why the author notes that new associations kept forming at the same rate.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 2, the sentence beginning "Nor could the persistence be attributed to mere habit."

breakdown.analysis: Paragraph 2 rules out explanations for why associations persisted, one per sentence. "Nor ... mere habit": if it were just old habit, existing groups might linger, but new ones wouldn't keep forming. Next sentence rules out distrust of banks. Prephrase: to rule out the habit explanation. Lesson: "Nor could X be attributed to Y" tells you the evidence is eliminating Y.

choices.note: Not the point. The program brought branches to nearly every district, and over half of vendors with accounts also joined associations.
Overstates. Same rate = steady demand, not growing popularity.
The trap. Ruling out distrust is the next sentence's job, using different evidence (members' views of bank safety).
The passage reports that vendors contribute more but explains it in P3. The new-formation rate doesn't explain it.
CORRECT. The sentence begins "Nor could the persistence be attributed to mere habit"; new associations forming shows active choice, which rules out habit as the explanation.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?
choices: A prevailing interpretation is described; evidence against it is presented; the interpretation is rejected in favor of an alternative the author argues applies generally.
A theory is described; evidence confirming the theory is presented; the theory is extended to a domain it did not originally address.

A prevailing interpretation and its prediction are described; evidence contrary to the prediction is presented and explained; the interpretation is credited with partial accuracy and its error identified.
A prediction is stated; the methods used to test it are criticized; an alternative method of testing it is proposed and applied.
