Two competing interpretations are described; evidence bearing on each is presented; the author concludes that neither can be evaluated without further study.
questions.explanation: The passage sets out Brandt’s interpretation and prediction, then presents and explains Valdora’s contrary evidence, then grants what Brandt got right while identifying his mistake. That is (C). (A) is the trap: the author does not reject the earlier interpretation outright, and declines to claim that the new account applies beyond Merovale. (E) misdescribes the passage, which presents only one interpretation in detail and reaches a definite conclusion.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Describe how the passage is organized.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: All four paragraphs: P1 Brandt's view and prediction, P2 contrary evidence, P3 explanation, P4 partial credit and error.

breakdown.analysis: Map: P1, Brandt's substitution view and its prediction (associations will wither). P2, Valdora's evidence that they didn't. P3, why: they protect savings. P4, Brandt was partly right; his mistake was inferring all their functions from where they first flourished. Prephrase: view + prediction, contrary evidence explained, view given partial credit and its error named. Lesson: check each step, especially the last; "rejected" vs. "partially credited" is the whole difference here.

choices.note: The trap. The author doesn't reject Brandt ("None of this implies that Brandt was simply wrong") and explicitly won't claim the new account applies beyond Merovale.
The evidence goes against Brandt's prediction, not for it.
CORRECT. Brandt's interpretation and prediction (P1), contrary evidence (P2) explained (P3), credit for partial accuracy and the error identified (P4).
The author doesn't criticize Valdora's methods. The single-city limit is noted, but the author says it's "enough" to show the substitution account is incomplete.
Only one interpretation is laid out as a rival theory, and the author reaches a definite conclusion: the substitution account is incomplete.

questions.stem: Which one of the following situations is most analogous to the point made in the last sentence of the passage?
choices: A town built a seawall to guard against storm surges; after a new offshore breakwater made the wall unnecessary for that purpose, residents kept maintaining it because it had become a valued promenade.
A company adopted a new accounting system because its old one was unreliable; when the new system also proved unreliable, the company returned to the old one.
A school introduced uniforms to reduce clothing costs for families; when uniform prices rose sharply, the school dropped its uniform requirement.
One species of bird migrates south each winter because food becomes scarce in the north; a related species that finds ample winter food in the north does not migrate.
A city banned cars from its central square to reduce air pollution; pollution in the square then fell, confirming that cars had been its main source.
questions.explanation: The last sentence says a practice adopted for one reason may persist for another, and that the second reason becomes visible only when the first disappears. In (A), the storm threat is removed, the wall is kept, and a second value is revealed. (D) is the strongest trap because it links a behavior to its reason, but it compares two species instead of showing one practice outliving its original rationale. (E) is a test that confirms the original reason rather than revealing a different one, and in (C) the practice is dropped rather than kept.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find the situation that matches the passage's last sentence.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 4, last sentence: "A practice adopted for one reason may persist for another, and only by observing what happens when the original reason disappears can the two be separated."

breakdown.analysis: Pattern: a practice starts for reason 1; reason 1 goes away; the practice continues, which reveals reason 2. Prephrase: something built for one purpose, that purpose disappears, and people keep it for a different value. Lesson: match all three steps of the pattern, not just "a thing and its reason."

choices.note: CORRECT. Seawall built for storms (reason 1); breakwater removes that need (reason disappears); residents keep it as a promenade (reason 2 revealed). Exactly the pattern.
The practice (new system) is dropped when it fails. Nothing persists for a new reason.
The practice is dropped, not kept. The opposite of persistence.
Strongest trap. It ties behavior to a reason, but compares two species instead of showing one practice outliving its original reason.
This confirms the original reason (cars caused the pollution). No second reason appears, and nothing persists after its reason is gone.

questions.stem: According to the passage, some vendors said that a pot received from a rotating association
choices: could not be spent before the next meeting without public embarrassment
was earmarked for a purpose that the group itself had chosen
was more likely to be spent on tempting purchases than a bank balance
was easier to decline to share because it was understood to be designated for a previously announced purpose
had to be returned to the association if it was not used for its announced purpose
questions.explanation: The third paragraph reports that some vendors found a pot ‘easier to refuse to share than a bank balance, because it was understood to be earmarked for a purpose announced to the group in advance,’ which is (D). (A) uses the passage’s own words in the wrong relationship: public embarrassment attaches to postponing a contribution, not to spending a pot. (B) misreads ‘announced to the group’ as ‘chosen by the group,’ and (E) adds an enforcement rule the passage never mentions.

setup.label: Task
setup.text: Find what some vendors said about a pot received from an association.

setup.label: Where to look
setup.text: Paragraph 3, last sentence.

breakdown.analysis: Near-quote: some vendors said a pot was "easier to refuse to share than a bank balance, because it was understood to be earmarked for a purpose announced to the group in advance." Prephrase: easier to say no to sharing because it was set aside for a pre-announced purpose. Lesson: watch small word changes ("announced to" vs. "chosen by").

choices.note: Wrong relationship. Public embarrassment attaches to postponing a contribution you owe, not to spending a pot you receive.
Misreads "announced to the group" as "chosen by the group." The member announced the purpose; the group didn't pick it.
Opposite. The pot is easier to protect, and tempting purchases were mentioned as a risk of bank money.
CORRECT. Matches the passage: a pot was "easier to refuse to share than a bank balance, because it was understood to be earmarked for a purpose announced to the group in advance."
No return rule is mentioned. Invented enforcement.

questions.stimulus: Curator: Critics have called the Halvorsen Museum's plan to rotate its textile collection every six months a gimmick designed to boost attendance. Admittedly, the rotation may well draw repeat visitors, and the museum's marketing office has said as much. But the rotation schedule is justified regardless of its effect on attendance. Many of the museum's textiles are colored with plant dyes that fade measurably even under low gallery lighting, and conservators recommend that such textiles be displayed for no more than six months in any two-year period. A six-month rotation is the only way the museum can display these textiles at all while honoring that recommendation.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the overall conclusion drawn in the curator's argument?
choices: Many of the museum's textiles are colored with plant dyes that fade under low gallery lighting.
The rotation plan will probably attract repeat visitors to the museum.
The plan to rotate the textile collection is warranted whether or not it boosts attendance.
Conservators' recommendations should determine how long any museum object is placed on display.
The museum cannot display its plant-dyed textiles at all unless it rotates them every six months.
questions.explanation: The curator's main claim, stated in the third sentence, is that the rotation is justified regardless of its effect on attendance; the dye and conservation facts support it, so C is correct. E is the claim that most directly supports the conclusion, not the conclusion itself. B echoes the concession, which the curator grants but does not argue for.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The six-month rotation is justified regardless of its effect on attendance.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Many textiles use plant dyes that fade even in low light; conservators recommend displaying such textiles no more than six months in any two years; a six-month rotation is the only way to show them at all within that limit.

breakdown.analysis: Same concession structure again: critics say gimmick; "Admittedly" it may draw repeat visitors; "But" it's justified regardless. Everything after the "But" sentence explains why. The last sentence (E) is the closest support, not the main point. It's like: "Sure, I enjoy the gym's smoothie bar. But my membership is worth it anyway: my doctor told me to exercise and it's the only gym near work."

choices.note: A premise. The fading dyes are the base fact that sets up the conservation argument.
This is the concession. The curator grants that rotation may draw repeat visitors but doesn't argue for it. Not the conclusion.
CORRECT. "Justified regardless of its effect on attendance" = warranted whether or not it boosts attendance. Everything about dyes and conservation exists to support this.
Way too broad. The curator talks about these fading textiles, not every museum object, and never says recommendations should determine display for everything.
Tempting because it's the last and strongest premise, but it's support. It explains why rotation is justified; it isn't the claim about justification itself.

questions.stimulus: In a survey of 400 adults, those who reported reading a printed book in bed before going to sleep also reported falling asleep faster, on average, than did those who reported using a phone in bed before going to sleep. The difference persisted even after the researchers took into account the respondents' ages and caffeine consumption. Clearly, then, reading a printed book at bedtime causes people to fall asleep faster than they otherwise would.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: overlooks the possibility that some factor not taken into account, such as a person's general level of stress, influences both the choice of bedtime activity and how quickly the person falls asleep
presumes without justification that every adult who uses a phone in bed has difficulty falling asleep
draws a conclusion about adults in general from a survey limited to adults who read printed books
takes for granted that reading a printed book is the only bedtime activity that helps people fall asleep
confuses a condition that is necessary for falling asleep quickly with one that is sufficient for doing so
questions.explanation: Controlling for age and caffeine does not rule out every common cause; a factor such as stress could drive both the choice of activity and sleep speed, which A identifies. C is wrong because the survey included phone users as well as readers. D misdescribes the argument, which says nothing about other activities being ineffective.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Reading a printed book at bedtime causes people to fall asleep faster than they otherwise would.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: In a survey of 400 adults, book readers in bed reported falling asleep faster than phone users in bed; the difference held after accounting for age and caffeine.

breakdown.analysis: Correlation to causation. The researchers controlled for two factors, but that doesn't rule out everything else. Maybe calmer people pick books and also fall asleep faster, while stressed people scroll their phones and lie awake. It's like noticing people who own yoga mats have lower blood pressure, controlling for age, and concluding mats lower blood pressure. Prephrase: a third factor drives both.

choices.note: CORRECT. Controlling for age and caffeine leaves other common causes open. Stress could push someone toward the phone and keep them awake. That third factor would produce the correlation without the book doing anything.
The argument compares averages. It never says every phone user has trouble sleeping.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Phone users fall asleep slower on average, so every single person who uses a phone in bed has insomnia.

choices.note: Factually wrong about the survey: it included phone users too, not just book readers.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: We surveyed only book club members and found they love reading, so most adults love reading.

choices.note: The argument says books help; it never says nothing else helps.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Reading helps you fall asleep, so reading is the only thing that can help you fall asleep.

choices.note: No necessary/sufficient language anywhere. The argument is about cause, not about conditions being required or enough.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: You need a dark room to fall asleep quickly, so anyone in a dark room will fall asleep quickly.

questions.stimulus: At the Larkspur Playhouse, every production that runs longer than four weeks is either a musical or a revival. No musical at the Playhouse is staged without a live orchestra. A revival is staged at the Playhouse only if the Playhouse's board approves it, and this season the board approved no revivals. This season, the Playhouse's production of The Glass Orchard is being staged without a live orchestra.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?
choices: The Glass Orchard is neither a musical nor a revival, so it is a new drama.
Every production staged at the Playhouse this season with a live orchestra is a musical.
Every musical staged at the Playhouse this season runs longer than four weeks.
The Glass Orchard does not run longer than four weeks this season.
If The Glass Orchard had been a revival, it would have run longer than four weeks.
questions.explanation: The Glass Orchard has no orchestra, so it is not a musical; there are no revivals this season, so it is not a revival; hence it cannot run longer than four weeks, which is D. B reverses a conditional: an orchestra is required for musicals, not limited to them. A is tempting because its first half must be true, but nothing says every other production is a new drama.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Runs > 4 weeks → musical OR revival; 2. Musical → live orchestra; 3. Revival staged → board approved it; 4. This season the board approved no revivals; 5. The Glass Orchard is being staged this season with no live orchestra.

breakdown.analysis: No orchestra → not a musical (contrapositive of 2). No board approval → no revivals this season → not a revival. Not musical AND not revival → doesn't run over four weeks (contrapositive of 1). It's like: you can stay after midnight only if you're staff or a VIP; you have no badge and no wristband, so you're out by midnight.

choices.note: Tempting because the first half must be true. But "so it's a new drama" assumes those are the only categories. It could be a comedy, an opera, anything.
Reverses a conditional. Musical → orchestra. That doesn't mean orchestra → musical; a play could use an orchestra too.
Reverses the first rule. Long runs must be musicals or revivals; that doesn't mean every musical has a long run.
CORRECT. No orchestra → not a musical. No approved revivals → not a revival. Not either → can't run longer than four weeks.
Reverses the first rule again. Being a revival is necessary for (part of) a long run, not sufficient. A revival can still have a short run.

questions.stimulus: Transit officials in the city of Corvale extended bus service on Route 9 so that it runs until 1 a.m. instead of 10 p.m. In the six months after the change, ridership on Route 9 during the original daytime hours rose by 12 percent. The officials concluded that the extended evening service made Route 9 more attractive even for daytime trips, presumably because riders who go out during the day can now count on a late ride home.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the officials' argument?
choices: Before the extension, Route 9's daytime ridership had been rising by roughly 2 percent every six months.
During the same six months, daytime ridership on Corvale bus routes whose hours were not extended remained essentially unchanged.
Corvale raised fares on all of its bus routes shortly before Route 9's hours were extended.
Several other cities have extended the hours of bus routes without seeing any increase in ridership.
Most riders who used Route 9 after 10 p.m. were commuting to or from night-shift jobs.
questions.explanation: B supplies a comparison group: routes without the extension saw no daytime gain, which makes it less likely that a citywide factor caused Route 9's increase. A is the tempting trap, but a 2 percent trend explains only a small part of a 12 percent rise and, if anything, slightly weakens the argument. E concerns late-night riders, not why daytime ridership rose.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Extending Route 9's evening service made it more attractive for daytime trips.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Route 9's hours went from 10 p.m. to 1 a.m.; in the next six months, daytime ridership on Route 9 rose 12%.

breakdown.analysis: Before/after with one cause blamed. What else could have pushed daytime ridership up? Gas prices, a new employer, citywide growth. The best strengthener is a control: routes without the extension saw no rise. Then citywide explanations fall away and the extension looks responsible. It's like a store adding late hours and seeing more daytime shoppers; it helps to know the other branches, without late hours, saw no change.

choices.note: Trap. A 2% background trend explains a small slice of a 12% jump. If anything it slightly weakens the argument by showing some of the rise would have happened anyway.
CORRECT. Same city, same six months, no extension, no daytime gain. That control group knocks out citywide causes and points at the extension.
Fare hikes on all routes would, if anything, push ridership down, and they hit every route equally. It doesn't explain why Route 9's daytime ridership rose.
Weakens. If other cities' extensions didn't raise ridership, that suggests extensions don't do much, which makes the officials' explanation less likely.
About who rides after 10 p.m. The conclusion is about why daytime ridership rose. Night-shift commuters don't explain daytime gains.

questions.stimulus: Paleontologist: Some researchers argue that the small theropod Ostranax hunted in packs, citing the discovery of several Ostranax skeletons together at the Dunmore quarry. But the fact that the skeletons were found together does not by itself establish that the animals lived together. Sediment analysis shows that the Dunmore site was a river bend where flowing water routinely deposited carcasses carried from many miles upstream, and bodies that accumulated in such a place could easily have come from animals that lived and died apart. So the Dunmore find provides little support for the pack-hunting hypothesis.
questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the role played in the argument by the claim that the fact that the skeletons were found together does not by itself establish that the animals lived together?
choices: It is the argument's overall conclusion.
It is the hypothesis that the argument is attempting to refute.
It is a premise that the researchers offer in support of the pack-hunting hypothesis.
It is offered as evidence that Ostranax did not hunt in packs.
It is supported by evidence in the argument and is in turn used to support the argument's overall conclusion.
questions.explanation: The sediment evidence supports the claim, and the claim in turn supports the conclusion that the find gives little support to the pack-hunting hypothesis, so it is an intermediate conclusion, as E says. D is the main trap: the argument never concludes that Ostranax did not hunt in packs, only that this find does not support the idea. A is wrong because the overall conclusion is the final sentence.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Dunmore find gives little support to the hypothesis that Ostranax hunted in packs.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Finding skeletons together doesn't by itself show the animals lived together; the site was a river bend where water deposited carcasses from far upstream, so they could have lived and died apart.

breakdown.analysis: Map the support. Sediment evidence (river bend collects carcasses) → supports "found together doesn't show lived together" → supports "the find provides little support for pack hunting." The claim in the question sits in the middle: it's supported and it supports. That's an intermediate conclusion. It's like: "The receipt is in your car; but that doesn't prove you bought it, because people toss receipts into cars all the time; so the receipt isn't good evidence you shopped there."

choices.note: The overall conclusion is the last sentence: the find gives little support to the pack-hunting hypothesis. The claim in question helps get there.
The hypothesis the paleontologist pushes back on is pack hunting. This claim is the paleontologist's own point, not the target.
Opposite. The researchers offer the skeletons being found together. This claim says that fact doesn't establish living together, which cuts against them.
Trap. The argument never concludes that Ostranax didn't hunt in packs, only that this find doesn't support the idea. Weak evidence for X isn't evidence against X.

CORRECT. The sediment analysis supports it (carcasses from far apart pile up there), and it in turn supports the final conclusion that the find gives little support to pack hunting. Intermediate conclusion.

questions.stimulus: Legislator: The proposed state tax on sugary beverages would raise the price of a typical soda by about 15 percent. Opponents argue that the tax would fall most heavily on low-income households. But all revenue from the tax is earmarked for subsidizing fresh produce sold in neighborhood groceries, which low-income households use disproportionately. Therefore, low-income households as a group would not be made financially worse off by the tax.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the legislator's argument depends?
choices: Low-income households purchase more sugary beverages than other households do.
The tax would reduce the consumption of sugary beverages among low-income households.
The amount low-income households as a group would save through the produce subsidies is not less than the amount they would pay in the new tax.
Fresh produce provides greater nutritional benefit than sugary beverages do.
Most of the revenue from the tax would be collected from households that are not low-income.
questions.explanation: For low-income households not to be worse off, their savings from the subsidies must at least match what they pay in the tax; if the savings were smaller, the conclusion would fail, so C is required. E is tempting but not necessary: even if low-income households paid most of the tax, they could still recoup it through the subsidies. A and D are not needed by the argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Low-income households as a group would not be made financially worse off by the sugary-beverage tax.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The tax raises soda prices about 15%; all revenue funds produce subsidies at neighborhood groceries, which low-income households use disproportionately.

breakdown.analysis: "Not worse off" is a net claim: what they get back must be at least what they pay. The legislator shows they'll get something back but never shows it's enough. So the argument needs: subsidy savings ≥ tax paid. It's like a landlord raising rent $100 and saying you're not worse off because he's giving you a free parking spot. That only works if the spot is worth at least $100 to you.

choices.note: Not needed. Whether they buy more soda than others doesn't matter; what matters is whether they get back at least what they pay. Negating it doesn't hurt (if anything it helps).
choices.negation: Low-income households do not purchase more sugary beverages than other households do.

choices.note: Not needed. Even if they keep drinking just as much soda, the subsidies could still cover the tax. Negating it doesn't break the argument.
choices.negation: The tax would not reduce the consumption of sugary beverages among low-income households.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: their subsidy savings are less than what they pay in tax. Then they're worse off, and the conclusion is dead. The argument needs this.
choices.negation: The amount low-income households as a group would save through the produce subsidies is less than the amount they would pay in the new tax.

choices.note: Nutrition is irrelevant to a claim about being financially worse off. Negating it changes nothing.
choices.negation: Fresh produce does not provide greater nutritional benefit than sugary beverages do.

choices.note: Tempting, since it would make low-income households' tax bill smaller. But not required: even if they paid most of the tax, the subsidies could still make them whole. Negating it doesn't kill the argument.
choices.negation: At least half of the revenue from the tax would be collected from low-income households.

questions.stimulus: Chemists found that compound Z breaks down in water faster in the presence of the catalyst Kenrite at 20°C than in the presence of Kenrite at 40°C. This result is surprising, because for nearly all chemical reactions, including the breakdown of compound Z when no catalyst is present, the reaction rate increases as temperature rises.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: Without a catalyst, compound Z breaks down faster at 40°C than at 20°C.
Above about 30°C, Kenrite particles clump together in water, greatly reducing the surface area available to interact with compound Z.
Kenrite is more expensive to produce than other catalysts that speed the breakdown of compound Z.
Many catalysts are more effective at higher temperatures than at lower temperatures.
Compound Z dissolves in water more slowly at 20°C than it does at 40°C.
questions.explanation: B gives a reason Kenrite becomes less effective at higher temperature, explaining why the catalyzed reaction is slower at 40°C despite the general trend. A merely restates part of the puzzle. D and E point the other way, making the result even more surprising.

setup.label: Paradox
setup.text: Almost all reactions, including Z's uncatalyzed breakdown, speed up as temperature rises, but with Kenrite, Z breaks down faster at 20°C than at 40°C.

breakdown.analysis: The reaction alone speeds up with heat, so something about the catalyst must go wrong at higher temperatures. Prephrase: Kenrite works worse when it's hot. It's like a bike being faster downhill, except your rider's tires go flat in the heat: the hill helps, but the bike still goes slower overall.

choices.note: Just restates part of the puzzle: we already know uncatalyzed Z breaks down faster when warmer. That's what makes the Kenrite result strange. No explanation.
CORRECT. Above about 30°C, Kenrite clumps and loses surface area, so it's a much weaker catalyst at 40°C. That loss can outweigh the general speed-up from heat.
Cost is irrelevant to reaction speed. Nothing about why the catalyzed reaction slows at higher temperature.
Makes it more puzzling. If catalysts generally work better when hotter, Kenrite's result is even stranger.
Also makes it more puzzling. If Z dissolves faster at 40°C, you'd expect the reaction to go faster there, not slower.

questions.stimulus: Arbitrator: Brellin Construction agreed to finish renovating the Oakfield community center by March 1 but did not finish until April 12. Brellin claims the delay resulted from its supplier's late delivery of steel beams. But Brellin's own records show that its crews were working on a different project for most of February. Clearly, then, the delay was caused by Brellin's diverting its crews to another project, not by the late delivery of steel.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the arbitrator's argument?
choices: Brellin has failed to meet completion deadlines on two other contracts in the past five years.
The contract specified a monetary penalty for each day the renovation remained unfinished after March 1.
The other project on which Brellin's crews worked in February was completed on schedule.
No work on the community center beyond what had been finished by February could proceed until the steel beams were installed, and the beams did not arrive until late March.
Brellin's steel supplier has delivered materials late to several other contractors in the region.
questions.explanation: D shows that the crews could not have advanced the project in February anyway, so the steel delay, not the reassignment, explains the late finish. E suggests the supplier is often late but does not show that its lateness caused this delay. A is about other contracts and, if anything, supports the arbitrator.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The delay was caused by Brellin diverting its crews to another project, not by the late steel delivery.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Brellin agreed to finish by March 1 but finished April 12; Brellin's records show its crews worked on another project for most of February.

breakdown.analysis: The arbitrator assumes the crews' absence mattered: that they could have been making progress in February. But what if no work was possible without the beams? Then keeping crews on site would have done nothing, and the steel is the real bottleneck. It's like blaming the cook for leaving the kitchen when the oven was broken: there was nothing to cook until it got fixed.

choices.note: If anything, a history of missed deadlines supports the idea that Brellin is at fault. It doesn't weaken the arbitrator, and it's about other contracts anyway.
A penalty clause just describes consequences. It says nothing about what caused the delay.
Shows the other project went fine, which says nothing about whether the community center was held up by crews or by steel.
CORRECT. No further work could happen until the beams were installed, and the beams arrived in late March. So the crews' February absence cost nothing; the steel delivery explains the April finish.
Tempting: the supplier is often late. But being late elsewhere doesn't show its lateness caused this delay, or that this delay couldn't have been avoided with the crews on site.

questions.stimulus: Theater critic: The Fenwick Repertory's new production of an eighteenth-century comedy has played to sold-out houses for three weeks. Some commentators attribute this success to the director's decision to reset the play in a modern corporate office. But this cannot be right. The Fenwick's previous production, which also reset a classic play in a modern setting, drew sparse audiences throughout its run.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the critic's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: presumes that a factor that failed to bring about a certain result in one case cannot have contributed to that result in another case
takes for granted that sold-out houses indicate that a production has been well received by critics
overlooks the possibility that the new production would have sold out even if it had kept its original setting
infers that the new production's success has no explanation from the fact that one proposed explanation for it is inadequate
attacks the commentators who made the attribution rather than addressing the attribution itself
questions.explanation: The critic rules out the modern setting as a cause of this success merely because it did not produce success in another production, ignoring that it could work in combination with other features here; A describes this. C is the most tempting trap, but that possibility would support the critic's conclusion rather than expose a flaw in it. D overstates the critic's conclusion, which rejects only one explanation and does not claim the success is unexplained.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The modern-office resetting can't be what made the new production a success.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The Fenwick's previous production also reset a classic play in a modern setting, and it drew sparse audiences.

breakdown.analysis: One failure doesn't show a factor can never contribute. A modern setting might work great with this script, this cast, this director, and flop with another. It's like saying hot sauce can't be why this taco is great because you once put hot sauce on oatmeal and it was terrible. Factors can work in combination.

choices.note: CORRECT. The critic reasons that because a modern setting didn't produce success last time, it can't have helped this time. That ignores that it could contribute together with other features of this production.
The argument is about audiences, not critics. Nobody equates sold-out houses with critical praise.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The show is sold out every night, so the critics must love it.

choices.note: Most tempting trap, but that possibility would help the critic: if it would have sold out anyway, the setting didn't cause the success. Pointing it out doesn't expose a flaw in the critic's reasoning.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Our new menu caused the rush of customers, ignoring that the rush happens every year during the festival.

choices.note: Overstates the critic's conclusion. The critic rejects one explanation; he never says the success has no explanation.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The director's resetting doesn't explain the show's success, so its success is a total mystery.

choices.note: The critic addresses the attribution itself with evidence (the previous production). No attack on the commentators.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Those commentators credit the modern setting, but they're all friends of the director, so they're wrong.

questions.stimulus: In a study at the Marlow Sleep Institute, participants deprived of sleep for one night performed worse on a memory test the next day than participants who had slept normally. Among the sleep-deprived participants, however, those who took a twenty-minute nap in the afternoon before the test performed as well as the well-rested participants on recalling facts, though not on recalling the order in which events occurred. Sleep-deprived participants who napped for longer than twenty minutes performed no better on either measure than those who napped for twenty minutes.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Naps longer than twenty minutes impair the memory of people who have been deprived of sleep.
Recalling the order in which events occurred depends on a stage of sleep that does not occur during short naps.
A twenty-minute nap is the most beneficial length of nap for people who have been deprived of sleep.
Sleep deprivation impairs the ability to recall facts more than it impairs the ability to recall the order of events.
Not every memory impairment caused by a night of sleep deprivation is reversed by an afternoon nap of twenty minutes or longer.
questions.explanation: Twenty-minute nappers still lagged on recalling event order, and longer nappers did no better than twenty-minute nappers, so no nap of twenty minutes or more reversed that impairment; E follows closely. C is the trap: shorter naps were never tested, and longer naps were equally good, so 'most beneficial' is unsupported. A overstates, since longer naps were no better, not worse.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. One night of sleep deprivation → worse next-day memory test than normal sleepers; 2. Deprived participants who took a 20-minute afternoon nap matched well-rested participants on fact recall, but not on recalling event order; 3. Deprived participants who napped longer than 20 minutes did no better on either measure than 20-minute nappers.

breakdown.analysis: Put 2 and 3 together. Twenty-minute nappers still lagged on event order. Longer nappers did no better than 20-minute nappers, so they lagged too. So no nap of 20 minutes or more fixed the event-order problem. That's one impairment a nap of that length didn't reverse. Notice the facts say nothing about naps under 20 minutes and don't say longer naps are worse, just not better.

choices.note: Overstates. Longer naps were "no better," not worse. Equal is not impaired.
Speculation about mechanism. The facts never mention sleep stages. Possible, but unsupported.
Trap. Shorter naps were never tested, and longer naps did just as well. So you can't call 20 minutes "most beneficial." At best it's tied for best among what was tested.
No comparison of how much each ability was impaired. A nap fixed fact recall, but that doesn't mean fact recall was hit harder. Unsupported.

CORRECT. Event-order recall stayed impaired after a 20-minute nap, and longer naps did no better. So at least one impairment wasn't reversed by a nap of 20 minutes or longer. "Not every" is safely modest.

questions.stimulus: Transit planner: Any proposed rail line that can be built within the city's current budget and that would reduce downtown traffic congestion deserves the city's support. The proposed Eastside light-rail line would reduce downtown congestion, since it would draw many commuters who now drive downtown. And the Eastside line's projected construction cost is lower than the cost of the recently completed Northgate line. So the Eastside line deserves the city's support.
questions.stem: The conclusion of the transit planner's argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Since its completion, the Northgate line has reduced downtown traffic congestion.
No rail line that the city's current budget is insufficient to build has a construction cost lower than that of the Northgate line.
Every rail line that deserves the city's support can be built within the city's current budget.
Most of the commuters who now drive downtown would switch to the Eastside line if it were built.
The Northgate line was built within the budget that the city had at the time of its construction.
questions.explanation: The principle requires both congestion reduction and affordability under the current budget. B, stated as a contrapositive, means any line cheaper than Northgate can be built within the current budget, which completes the argument. E is the strongest trap but concerns the budget at the time Northgate was built, not the current one. C reverses the principle's conditional.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Eastside line deserves the city's support.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Buildable within current budget AND reduces downtown congestion → deserves support; Eastside would reduce congestion by drawing drivers; Eastside's projected cost is lower than the recently completed Northgate line's cost.

breakdown.analysis: Two conditions: reduces congestion (given) and buildable within the current budget (not given). We only know Eastside is cheaper than Northgate. Bridge needed: cheaper than Northgate → buildable within the current budget. B says: budget insufficient → not cheaper than Northgate. Contrapositive: cheaper than Northgate → current budget is sufficient. Chain: Eastside cheaper → within budget; + reduces congestion → deserves support. It's like: you can buy anything that's affordable and useful; this is cheaper than your last purchase; that only helps if anything cheaper than your last purchase is affordable right now.

choices.note: Irrelevant. How Northgate performed doesn't establish anything about Eastside's affordability, the missing condition.
CORRECT. Contrapositive: cost lower than Northgate → can be built within the current budget. Eastside is cheaper, so it's within budget; it also reduces congestion; so it deserves support.

Reverses the principle. The rule says affordable + helpful → deserves support. C says deserves support → affordable. That's a necessary condition, and it doesn't help us prove Eastside deserves support.
Just bolsters the congestion premise, which is already given. The missing piece is the budget.
Strongest trap. It's about the budget back when Northgate was built, not the current budget. Budgets change, so this doesn't close the gap.

questions.stimulus: A party to a contract who fails to perform an obligation should be excused from liability for that failure only if the failure resulted from circumstances that the party could not reasonably have foreseen when the contract was signed and the party took reasonable steps to limit the resulting harm.
questions.stem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?
choices: A caterer that failed to deliver food for a banquet because of a sudden road closure, and that tried every available alternate route, should be excused from liability.
A printer that missed a deadline because its press broke down unexpectedly should be excused from liability, since the breakdown could not have been foreseen.
A landscaper that failed to finish a job by the agreed date because the region's rainy season began at its usual time should not be excused from liability.
A supplier whose deliveries were late because of a strike announced months before the contract was signed should be excused, since it hired replacement drivers promptly.
A musician who canceled a contracted performance because of a sudden illness should not be excused from liability, since the illness could not have been foreseen.
questions.explanation: The principle states only necessary conditions for excusal. A rainy season that began at its usual time was foreseeable, so the landscaper fails a necessary condition and should not be excused, as C says. A is the main trap: the caterer meets both conditions, but under an 'only if' principle that does not establish that excusal is warranted. D excuses a party whose failure stemmed from foreseeable circumstances, and E treats unforeseeability as a reason against excusal.

setup.label: Principle
setup.text: Excused from liability → failure resulted from circumstances not reasonably foreseeable at signing AND the party took reasonable steps to limit the harm. Contrapositive: foreseeable circumstances OR no reasonable mitigation → not excused.

breakdown.analysis: "Only if" makes these necessary conditions. So the principle can only tell you someone should NOT be excused (when a condition fails). It can never tell you someone SHOULD be excused. Look for a "should not be excused" where foreseeability or mitigation fails. It's like "you get a refund only if you have the receipt and return within 30 days." No receipt → no refund. Receipt and on time → still not guaranteed.

choices.note: Main trap. The caterer meets both conditions: an unforeseeable road closure and trying every route. But meeting necessary conditions doesn't guarantee excusal. The principle can't support "should be excused."
Same problem, worse. It concludes "should be excused" from unforeseeability alone, without even mentioning mitigation. The principle never makes anyone excused.
CORRECT. A rainy season that began at its usual time was foreseeable. That fails a necessary condition, so the landscaper should not be excused. Exactly what the contrapositive gives.
The strike was announced months before signing, so it was foreseeable. That fails a necessary condition, meaning the supplier should not be excused. D says the opposite.
Backwards logic. Unforeseeability is one of the things that helps a party; the principle never treats it as a reason against excusal.

questions.stimulus:
Ilse: Museums should display skilled reproductions of fragile artifacts rather than the originals. Visitors come to museums to learn about the past, and a skilled reproduction conveys the same information as the original while sparing the original from deterioration.

Tomas: Visitors gain something from standing before an actual object that no copy can provide: a sense of direct connection to the people who made it. Fragile originals must of course be protected, but they can be shown under controlled conditions for limited periods rather than being replaced by copies.
questions.stem: Ilse and Tomas disagree over whether
choices: fragile artifacts need to be protected from deterioration
visitors come to museums primarily to learn about the past
a skilled reproduction can convey the same information as the original artifact
displaying fragile originals under controlled conditions is sufficient to protect them
museums should display reproductions of fragile artifacts in place of the originals
questions.explanation: Ilse says museums should display reproductions instead of fragile originals; Tomas says the originals can be shown and should not be replaced, so they disagree about E. C is a trap: Tomas does not deny that copies convey the same information, only that information is all visitors gain. Both agree on A, and Ilse says nothing about D.

setup.label: Arguments
setup.text: Ilse: Museums should display skilled reproductions instead of fragile originals; they convey the same information and spare the originals.; Tomas: Originals give a sense of direct connection no copy can; fragile ones should be shown under controlled conditions for limited periods rather than replaced by copies.

breakdown.analysis: To disagree, one speaker must say yes and the other no. Ilse: yes, replace fragile originals with copies. Tomas: no, show the originals carefully instead. That's the fight. Tomas never denies that copies carry the same information; he says information isn't all visitors get. It's like one friend saying "just stream the concert, the music's identical" and the other saying "sure, but you miss being there."

choices.note: Both agree. Ilse wants to spare originals from deterioration; Tomas says fragile originals "must of course be protected."
Only Ilse says this. Tomas talks about a sense of connection but never denies that people come to learn. No clear disagreement.
Trap. Tomas doesn't deny copies convey the same information. He says visitors gain something beyond information. Different point, not a no.
Only Tomas raises controlled conditions. Ilse says nothing about whether they're enough, so we can't say she disagrees.
CORRECT. Ilse: museums should show reproductions in place of fragile originals. Tomas: originals should be shown under controlled conditions, "rather than being replaced by copies." Clean yes vs. no.

questions.stimulus: Some chemists have claimed that the green tint in the glaze of ancient Torvan pottery came from copper that potters added deliberately. But if the copper had been added deliberately, we would expect the tint to be roughly uniform among pots from the same workshop, since Torvan potters followed fixed glaze recipes. In fact, pots from a single workshop vary widely in tint, and the variation closely tracks the copper content of the local clay deposits from which each batch of clay was dug. Thus the copper most likely entered the glaze unintentionally, from the clay itself.
questions.stem: The argument proceeds by
choices: showing that a consequence to be expected if a hypothesis were true is not borne out, and offering an alternative explanation that fits the evidence
questioning the expertise of the chemists who proposed a hypothesis in order to cast doubt on that hypothesis
arguing that a hypothesis must be false because one of its predictions fails, and concluding that the only possible alternative hypothesis must therefore be true
drawing a general conclusion about all ancient pottery from evidence concerning a single workshop
demonstrating that the evidence the chemists cited in support of their hypothesis is inaccurate
questions.explanation: The argument notes that deliberate addition predicts uniform tint, observes that tint is not uniform, and proposes that copper came from the clay, which fits the observed variation, as A describes. C is the closest trap, but the argument does not claim its alternative is the only possible one or that it must be true; it says 'most likely' and supports it with the clay-content evidence. E is wrong because the argument does not dispute the chemists' evidence.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The copper most likely entered the Torvan glaze unintentionally, from the clay.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: If copper were added deliberately, tint should be roughly uniform within a workshop (fixed recipes); instead, tint varies widely within workshops, tracking the copper content of each batch's local clay.

breakdown.analysis: Two moves. First: the chemists' hypothesis predicts uniform tint; tint isn't uniform, so the prediction fails. Second: offer a rival explanation (copper from the clay) that fits the evidence, including the tracking with clay copper. And it's hedged: "most likely." It's like: if Dad made all the cookies with his recipe, they'd taste the same; they vary a lot, and the saltier ones came from the batch with the salted butter, so the butter probably explains it.

choices.note: CORRECT. Expected consequence of deliberate addition (uniform tint) isn't borne out; the alternative (copper from clay) fits the variation. Exactly the two moves the argument makes.
The chemists' expertise is never questioned. The argument deals with evidence only.
choices.example: Example of this method: These chemists mostly study modern plastics, so their claim about ancient glazes shouldn't be trusted.

choices.note: Closest trap. The argument says "most likely," not "must," and never claims the clay explanation is the only possible alternative. It supports it with evidence instead of by elimination.
choices.example: Example of this method: The copper wasn't added on purpose, so the only other option is that it came from the clay, and therefore it definitely did.

choices.note: No generalization to all ancient pottery. The argument is about Torvan pottery only.
choices.example: Example of this method: This one Torvan workshop's glaze got its copper from clay, so every ancient pottery glaze got its color from clay.

choices.note: The argument doesn't say the chemists' evidence is wrong. It introduces new evidence (tint variation, clay copper) that cuts against their hypothesis.
choices.example: Example of this method: The chemists claim the pots contain copper, but their measurements were badly calibrated, so the data is unreliable.

questions.stimulus: Economist: When the province of Ardell cut its tax rate on corporate profits last year, opponents of the cut predicted that it would reduce the province's revenue from corporate taxes. Yet in the year following the cut, Ardell's total revenue from corporate taxes actually rose. So the opponents' prediction was mistaken: the tax cut did not reduce the province's corporate tax revenue.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the economist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: takes for granted that the opponents of the tax cut had no reasonable basis for their prediction
overlooks the possibility that revenue rose because corporations relocated to Ardell in response to the lower rate
draws a conclusion about tax policy in general from evidence concerning a single province
fails to consider that the province's corporate tax revenue might have risen even more had the tax rate not been cut
attacks the motives of those who opposed the tax cut rather than the substance of their prediction
questions.explanation: Revenue rising after the cut does not show the cut failed to reduce revenue relative to what it would otherwise have been, perhaps because of general economic growth; D identifies this overlooked possibility. B is the trap: relocation spurred by the cut would mean the cut raised revenue, supporting the economist rather than exposing a flaw. C is wrong because the economist draws no conclusion beyond Ardell.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The tax cut did not reduce Ardell's corporate tax revenue; the opponents' prediction was mistaken.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Ardell cut its corporate tax rate; in the following year, its total corporate tax revenue rose.

breakdown.analysis: "Reduce revenue" means compared with what would have happened without the cut. Revenue rising doesn't show that. If the economy boomed, revenue might have risen 20% without the cut and only 5% with it. The cut still cost money. It's like saying skipping the gym didn't hurt your fitness because you got fitter this year, when you were training for a marathon anyway.

choices.note: The economist says the prediction was wrong, not that it was unreasonable. No assumption about the opponents' basis.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The forecasters predicted rain and it didn't rain, so they had no good reason to predict rain.

choices.note: Trap. If companies moved in because of the lower rate, the cut actually raised revenue, which supports the economist. That's not a flaw in the reasoning.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Sales rose after our new ad, so the ad worked, overlooking that a competitor closed the same week.

choices.note: The conclusion is only about Ardell. No generalization to tax policy everywhere.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: Ardell's tax cut didn't lower revenue, so tax cuts never lower revenue anywhere.

choices.note: CORRECT. Revenue might have risen even more without the cut, for example because of economic growth. Then the cut did reduce revenue compared to the alternative, and the opponents were right.
No mention of anyone's motives. The economist addresses the prediction with data.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The opponents only predicted lost revenue because they wanted to embarrass the governor, so their prediction was wrong.

questions.stimulus: Fossil pollen from a lake bed in the Serrin Basin shows that the region's forest gave way to grassland about 8,000 years ago. Charcoal layers in the same lake bed show that frequent fires began about 8,300 years ago. Some researchers conclude that a drying climate caused the shift to grassland. But the fires began before the forest declined, and frequent fires are known to prevent forest regrowth. Therefore, it was the fires, rather than climatic drying, that were primarily responsible for the shift to grassland.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: Grasslands are less susceptible to fire than are forests.
Climatic drying was not the principal reason that fires became frequent in the Serrin Basin about 8,300 years ago.
Fires have remained frequent in the Serrin Basin ever since the forest was replaced by grassland.
No significant climatic drying occurred in the Serrin Basin around the time the forest gave way to grassland.
No region other than the Serrin Basin experienced a shift from forest to grassland about 8,000 years ago.
questions.explanation: If drying caused the fires, then drying would be the underlying cause of the shift, and the argument's contrast between fires and drying would collapse; so the argument requires B. D is the main trap but is too strong: the argument claims only that fires were the primary cause, which is compatible with some drying having occurred. A, C, and E concern matters the argument need not address.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Fires, rather than climatic drying, were primarily responsible for the Serrin Basin's shift from forest to grassland.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Frequent fires began about 8,300 years ago; the forest gave way to grassland about 8,000 years ago; frequent fires are known to prevent forest regrowth.

breakdown.analysis: The argument pits fires against drying as rival causes. But what if drying caused the fires? Then drying is the real root cause and fires are just the middle link, so "fires rather than drying" falls apart. The argument must assume drying wasn't what made the fires frequent. It's like blaming a flat tire rather than the nail for being late, when the nail caused the flat.

choices.note: Not needed. Whether grasslands burn less doesn't affect whether fires drove the forest out. Negating it doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: Grasslands are at least as susceptible to fire as forests are.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: drying was the main reason fires became frequent. Then drying is the underlying cause of the shift, and "fires rather than drying" collapses.
choices.negation: Climatic drying was the principal reason that fires became frequent in the Serrin Basin about 8,300 years ago.

choices.note: Not needed. The argument is about what caused the shift, not what happened afterward. Fires could have stopped later and the argument is fine.
choices.negation: Fires have not remained frequent in the Serrin Basin since the forest was replaced by grassland.

choices.note: Main trap. Too strong. The argument says fires were the primary cause, which fits with some drying happening too. Negate it (some drying occurred) and the argument survives, as long as drying didn't cause the fires.
choices.negation: Some significant climatic drying occurred in the Serrin Basin around the time the forest gave way to grassland.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Other regions don't matter to what caused this region's shift. Negating it does nothing.
choices.negation: Some region other than the Serrin Basin experienced a shift from forest to grassland about 8,000 years ago.

questions.stimulus: Every actor in the Brightwater Players' spring season appeared in at least one of its two productions, Mariner and The Tollkeeper, and no actor appeared in both. All of the actors in Mariner had trained at the Calder Studio, as had some of the actors in The Tollkeeper. None of the actors who trained at the Calder Studio was under 25 years old. Every actor in the season who was under 25 had trained at either the Calder Studio or the Ines Workshop.
questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following CANNOT be true?
choices: Some actor in Mariner had trained at the Ines Workshop.
Every actor in The Tollkeeper had trained at the Calder Studio.
No actor in the spring season had trained at the Ines Workshop.
Every actor in the spring season who was under 25 appeared in The Tollkeeper.
Some actor in the spring season who was under 25 did not appear in The Tollkeeper.
questions.explanation: An actor who did not appear in The Tollkeeper must have appeared in Mariner, and so trained at Calder and was not under 25; thus E cannot be true. D is the trap, but it actually must be true by the same reasoning. A is a second trap: nothing restricts the Ines Workshop to actors under 25, so a Mariner actor over 25 could have trained at both schools. B and C are consistent with the statements (C holds if no actor was under 25).

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Every actor was in exactly one of Mariner or The Tollkeeper; 2. All Mariner actors trained at Calder; some Tollkeeper actors trained at Calder; 3. Calder-trained → not under 25; 4. Under 25 → trained at Calder or Ines.

breakdown.analysis: Chain it. Mariner → Calder → not under 25. Contrapositive: under 25 → not in Mariner → (exactly one play) → in The Tollkeeper. So every under-25 actor was in The Tollkeeper. An answer saying some under-25 actor wasn't in The Tollkeeper is impossible. For a cannot-be-true question, anything merely possible is wrong. It's like: everyone on the bus is an adult; every person here is on either the bus or the train; so every kid here is on the train.

choices.note: Possible. Nothing limits Ines to under-25 actors, so a Mariner actor over 25 could have trained at both Calder and Ines. Second trap: it feels forbidden but isn't.
Possible. We're told some Tollkeeper actors trained at Calder; nothing stops all of them from having trained there (as long as none is under 25).
Possible. If no actor was under 25, the Ines rule never comes into play, and nobody needs to have trained there.
Trap. This is not just possible; it must be true. Under 25 → not Calder → not Mariner → Tollkeeper. A must-be-true statement can't be the answer to a cannot-be-true question.
CORRECT. An under-25 actor not in The Tollkeeper would have to be in Mariner, so trained at Calder, so not under 25. Contradiction. This cannot be true.

questions.stimulus: Researchers at Penwick University found that office workers whose desks were next to windows slept, on average, 40 minutes longer per night than coworkers whose desks were in windowless interior areas. The researchers hypothesize that daytime exposure to natural light helps regulate the body's internal clock, thereby improving nighttime sleep.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the researchers' argument?
choices: Workers with desks next to windows reported higher job satisfaction than did workers with interior desks.
Desks next to windows were assigned mostly to senior employees, who tend to work shorter hours than other employees.
Workers whose desks were next to north-facing windows that admitted little daylight slept no longer, on average, than workers with interior desks.
Exposure to bright artificial light in the evening is known to make it harder for people to fall asleep.
Most of the workers studied slept longer on weekend nights than on weeknights.
questions.explanation: C shows that the sleep advantage disappears when window desks receive little daylight, tying the effect to light exposure rather than to anything else about window desks. D is the trap: it links light and sleep, but concerns evening artificial light, not daytime natural light. B weakens the argument, and A offers another difference between the groups that could itself explain the gap.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Daytime exposure to natural light helps regulate the body clock and improves nighttime sleep (explaining why window-desk workers sleep longer).

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Penwick office workers at window desks slept on average 40 minutes longer per night than coworkers at interior desks.

breakdown.analysis: Window desks differ from interior desks in lots of ways: view, status, who gets them, noise. The researchers say it's the daylight. Strongest help: hold "window desk" fixed and vary the light. If window desks with little daylight show no sleep benefit, light really is the ingredient. It's like testing whether it's the coffee or the café that wakes you up: sit in the café drinking decaf.

choices.note: Weakens if anything: higher job satisfaction is another difference between the groups that could itself explain better sleep.
Weakens. Senior employees working shorter hours is an alternate explanation for sleeping longer, unrelated to light.
CORRECT. North-facing windows: still a window desk, but little daylight, and no sleep advantage. That isolates daylight as the factor, ruling out other features of window desks.
Trap. It links light to sleep, but it's evening artificial light making sleep harder. The hypothesis is about daytime natural light helping. Different light, different time, different direction.
Weekend vs. weeknight sleep applies to everyone. It says nothing about window vs. interior desks or daylight.

questions.stimulus: If the Kessling ferry service adds a midday crossing, then it will either hire another pilot or reduce its evening service. The ferry service will not reduce its evening service unless the regional council approves the reduction, and the council will not approve it. So if the ferry service adds a midday crossing, it will hire another pilot.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its pattern of reasoning to the argument above?
choices: If Dana enrolls in the summer course, she will either quit her part-time job or take out a loan. She will not take out a loan unless her parents cosign it, and they will not cosign it. So if Dana enrolls in the summer course, she will quit her part-time job.

If the library extends its hours, it will either hire new staff or move current staff to evenings. It will move staff to evenings only if the union agrees, and the union will agree. So if the library extends its hours, it will move current staff to evenings.

The orchard will either hire seasonal pickers or leave some fruit unharvested. It will not leave fruit unharvested unless prices fall, and prices will not fall. So the orchard will hire seasonal pickers.

If the museum renovates its west wing, it will either close the wing or move its exhibits. It will not close the wing unless attendance drops, and attendance will drop. So the museum will close the west wing.

If the band tours in the spring, it will both rent a bus and hire a driver. It will not hire a driver unless its label pays for one, and the label will not pay. So the band will not tour in the spring.
questions.explanation: A matches the structure exactly: if X then Y or Z; not Z unless W; not W; so if X then Y. C is the trap: it uses the same disjunction-elimination step but lacks the opening conditional and draws an unconditional conclusion. B and D conclude the eliminable disjunct from an affirmed condition, and E uses a conjunction and concludes by denying the antecedent.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: If the ferry service adds a midday crossing, it will hire another pilot.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Midday crossing → hire pilot OR reduce evening service; reduce evening → council approves; council won't approve.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: If X, then Y or Z; Z only if W; not W; so if X, then Y.

breakdown.analysis: Valid argument. No council approval → no evening reduction → the "or" collapses to hiring a pilot. Keep the conditional frame: the conclusion is still "if midday crossing, then pilot." Match all four parts: opening conditional with an either/or, "not Z unless W," "not W," and a conditional conclusion naming the other option.

choices.note: CORRECT. Enroll → quit job OR loan; loan → parents cosign; parents won't; so enroll → quit job. Same four pieces, same conditional conclusion.

Breaks the pattern. It affirms the condition (union will agree) and then concludes that option happens. But "only if" means union agreement is necessary, not sufficient. Flawed, and it concludes the wrong disjunct.
Trap. Same elimination step (not Z unless W; not W; so Y), but there's no opening "if" and the conclusion is unconditional. The original's conclusion is conditional. Close, not the same.
Affirms the condition (attendance will drop) and concludes the museum will close the wing. Necessary isn't sufficient, and the conclusion isn't conditional. Different and flawed.
Uses "both...and" instead of "either...or," and concludes the band won't tour. That's a different structure (knocking out a required part kills the plan).

questions.stimulus: Museum director: Last year we replaced the printed wall labels in our ceramics gallery with a free smartphone app that provides far more detailed information about each piece. Our data show that the average time visitors spend in that gallery has since increased from 6 minutes to 11 minutes. Clearly, the app has made visitors more engaged with the ceramics on display.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the museum director's argument?
choices: In a survey, most visitors who used the app said they preferred it to the printed labels.
Overall attendance at the museum rose slightly last year.
The average time visitors spend in the museum's other galleries did not change last year.
The 11-minute figure comes from the app's own usage logs and so reflects only visitors who chose to download the app, whereas the 6-minute figure was based on a sample of all visitors to the gallery.
The app offers information in six languages, whereas the printed labels were available in only one.
questions.explanation: D shows that the comparison is between different populations: app users are self-selected and likely more interested to begin with, so the increase may not reflect any change the app produced. C is the trap; it actually strengthens the argument by ruling out a museum-wide trend. E, if anything, suggests a reason the app might increase engagement, and B concerns the number of visitors rather than how long each stays.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The smartphone app has made visitors more engaged with the ceramics.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Printed labels were replaced with a detailed free app; average gallery time rose from 6 minutes to 11 minutes.

breakdown.analysis: Check whether the two numbers measure the same people. If the before figure covers everyone and the after figure covers only people who chose to download the app, you're comparing all visitors to the keenest ones. Of course the keen ones stay longer. It's like comparing average gym time for all members last year to average time this year for people who signed up for the personal training plan.

choices.note: Liking the app isn't the same as being more engaged with the ceramics, but it doesn't hurt the argument either. If anything it's mildly supportive.
More visitors doesn't change how long each one stays. Average time is unaffected by headcount.
Trap: it strengthens. If other galleries saw no change, a museum-wide trend can't explain the ceramics jump, which points to the app.

CORRECT. The 11-minute number comes only from people who chose to download the app, the self-selected keen visitors. The 6-minute number covers everyone. That's apples to oranges; the jump may reflect who's counted, not what the app did.
If anything, more languages gives a reason the app could increase engagement. It supports, not weakens.

questions.stimulus: Any compound that is stable at room temperature and does not react with water can be stored safely in the laboratory's general cabinet. Compound R7 does not react with water. Moreover, every compound synthesized by the Oduya method is stable at room temperature unless it contains a nitro group. Therefore, compound R7 can be stored safely in the general cabinet.
questions.stem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?
choices: Every compound that contains a nitro group reacts with water.
Compound R7 was synthesized by the Oduya method.
Any compound that does not react with water and contains no nitro group is stable at room temperature.
Every compound that can be stored safely in the general cabinet is stable at room temperature.
Compound R7 was synthesized by the Oduya method, and no compound that contains a nitro group fails to react with water.
questions.explanation: The argument needs R7 to be stable at room temperature. Under E, since R7 does not react with water it contains no nitro group (contrapositive), and as an Oduya compound without a nitro group it is stable, so the conclusion follows. A and B are the traps: each supplies only half of this chain. C would still require knowing that R7 lacks a nitro group, and D reverses the first conditional.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Compound R7 can be stored safely in the general cabinet.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Stable at room temp AND doesn't react with water → safe in general cabinet; R7 doesn't react with water; Oduya compound → stable unless it contains a nitro group.

breakdown.analysis: We have "no water reaction." We need "stable." Oduya rule: Oduya AND no nitro → stable. So we need R7 to be (1) an Oduya compound and (2) nitro-free. E gives both: R7 is Oduya, and nitro → reacts with water. Contrapositive: doesn't react with water → no nitro. Chain: R7 doesn't react → no nitro; Oduya + no nitro → stable; stable + doesn't react → safe in cabinet. It's like needing both a ticket and an ID: a sufficient answer has to hand you both.

choices.note: Trap. Gives you "no nitro" (doesn't react → no nitro), but not that R7 is an Oduya compound. Without Oduya, the stability rule never applies.
Trap. Gives you Oduya, but not that R7 lacks a nitro group. If it has one, it might be unstable.
Would work only if we knew R7 has no nitro group, and we don't. Still a missing link.
Reverses the first conditional. It says safe → stable, which is a necessary condition. We need to prove R7 is safe, not use safety as a starting point.
CORRECT. R7 is Oduya; nitro → reacts with water, so R7 (no water reaction) has no nitro; Oduya + no nitro → stable; stable + no water reaction → safe in the general cabinet.

questions.stimulus: Fossil footprints of the dinosaur Merrovar are common in the Callan Formation, but Merrovar skeletal remains have rarely been found there. By contrast, skeletal remains of the plant-eater Tessaurus are abundant in the formation, while Tessaurus footprints are almost entirely absent. Footprints are best preserved in moist mudflats, whereas skeletons are best preserved where carcasses are rapidly buried in sediment, as in river channels during floods.
questions.stem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?
choices: Fewer Merrovar than Tessaurus lived in the region where the Callan Formation was deposited.
The relative numbers of a species' footprints and skeletal remains in a fossil deposit may depend partly on the environments in which members of that species lived or died.
The Callan Formation contains deposits that formed both in moist mudflats and in river channels.
If Merrovar had frequented river channels during floods, Merrovar skeletal remains would be abundant in the Callan Formation.
Most dinosaur species are better represented in the fossil record by skeletons than by footprints.
questions.explanation: Because footprints and skeletons are best preserved in different settings, the contrasting patterns for the two species suggest that where each species spent time or died affected what was preserved, which supports the hedged claim in B. C is the main trap: the stimulus says only where footprints and skeletons are best preserved and gives river channels merely as an example of rapid burial, so it does not establish that both kinds of deposit are present. D overstates by turning a tendency into a guarantee, and A ignores that preservation, not population size, may explain the pattern.

setup.label: Facts
setup.text: 1. Merrovar footprints are common in the Callan Formation, but its skeletons are rare; 2. Tessaurus skeletons are abundant there, but its footprints are almost absent; 3. Footprints preserve best in moist mudflats; skeletons preserve best where carcasses are quickly buried, as in flooding river channels.

breakdown.analysis: Two species, opposite patterns, and two different best-preservation settings. The natural takeaway: where an animal spent its time or died may shape which kind of fossil it leaves. Mudflat walkers leave tracks; animals that die in floods leave bones. Note how modest the right answer should be: "may depend partly." It's like a museum having lots of a famous person's letters but no photos: maybe they wrote a lot and avoided cameras.

choices.note: Ignores the preservation story. Merrovar footprints are common, so plenty of Merrovar were around. Fewer skeletons could just reflect where they died, not how many lived.

CORRECT. Footprints and skeletons preserve best in different settings, and the two species show opposite patterns. So the environments a species lived or died in may partly drive its mix of tracks and bones. Hedged and well supported.

Main trap. The facts say where each kind of fossil preserves best, and river channels are only an example of rapid burial. That doesn't establish that the formation actually contains both mudflat and river-channel deposits.
Overstates. Preservation conditions are a tendency ("best preserved"), not a guarantee. Frequenting river channels wouldn't make abundant skeletons certain.
Goes way beyond the facts. Two species in one formation say nothing about most dinosaur species.

questions.stimulus: Attorney: My client, Ms. Reyes, contracted to buy the Halden Street house 'subject to a satisfactory inspection.' The inspector found a hairline crack in the foundation, and Ms. Reyes withdrew from the purchase. The seller contends that the inspection was satisfactory, since the inspector's report concluded that the house is 'structurally sound overall.' But an inspection that reveals a cracked foundation cannot be considered satisfactory. After all, any reasonable buyer would feel some concern on learning that a house's foundation is cracked.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the attorney's argument is flawed in that it
choices: relies on the seller's interpretation of the contract's language while claiming to reject it
attempts to discredit the seller's position by questioning the seller's motives
treats a finding's being a reasonable cause for some concern as though that alone established that the contract's condition was not met
uses the term 'satisfactory' in one sense in a premise and in a different sense in the conclusion
presumes that the inspector's overall conclusion about the house's structural soundness was false
questions.explanation: The attorney moves from the claim that a reasonable buyer would feel some concern to the conclusion that the inspection was unsatisfactory, without showing that mere concern makes an inspection unsatisfactory; C describes this gap. D is tempting because the attorney and seller understand 'satisfactory' differently, but the attorney's own argument uses the term in only one sense, so there is no equivocation within it. E fails because the attorney's argument is compatible with the house being structurally sound overall.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: An inspection that reveals a cracked foundation can't be considered satisfactory, so Reyes could withdraw.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The contract was subject to a satisfactory inspection; the inspector found a hairline foundation crack; any reasonable buyer would feel some concern on learning a foundation is cracked.

breakdown.analysis: Gap: "a reasonable buyer would feel some concern" → "the inspection wasn't satisfactory." Those aren't the same. Plenty of satisfactory inspections turn up something mildly worrying. The attorney never shows that any concern at all makes an inspection unsatisfactory. It's like saying a job interview went badly because any reasonable candidate would feel a bit nervous about one tough question.

choices.note: The attorney doesn't rely on the seller's reading. The attorney uses a different standard (reasonable buyer concern).
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The seller says "satisfactory" means structurally sound; the house is structurally sound by that standard, so my client was right to withdraw.
