choices.note: No attack on the seller's motives anywhere. The attorney argues about what counts as satisfactory.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The seller only calls the inspection satisfactory because he wants the money, so it wasn't satisfactory.

choices.note: CORRECT. Feeling some concern is treated as enough to make the inspection unsatisfactory. The attorney never shows that mere concern means the contract's condition wasn't met.
Tempting, because the attorney and seller mean different things by "satisfactory." But within the attorney's own argument, the word is used in only one sense. No equivocation inside the argument.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The report was satisfactory, meaning it was complete; satisfactory reports mean the house is fine; so the house is fine.

choices.note: The attorney never denies the house is structurally sound overall. The argument is compatible with that: a house can be sound and still have an unsatisfactory inspection under the attorney's view.
choices.example: Example of this flaw: The foundation has a crack, so the inspector was simply wrong that the house is structurally sound.

questions.stimulus: Columnist: The town of Bramwell is considering exempting groceries from its sales tax. Supporters point out that low-income residents spend a larger share of their income on groceries than other residents do. But the exemption would also reduce grocery taxes for wealthy residents, and the lost revenue would come largely out of the town's library and park budgets, on which low-income residents rely heavily. A direct rebate to low-income residents would help them at least as much at a fraction of the cost. So Bramwell should not adopt the grocery exemption.
questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the columnist's reasoning?
choices: A government should not adopt a measure intended to benefit a particular group if a less costly alternative would benefit that group at least as much without reducing services the group depends on.
A sales tax should never be imposed on goods that are necessities for most residents of a community.
A proposed change in tax policy should be evaluated solely according to its effect on a government's total revenue.
A town government should give funding for libraries and parks priority over providing tax relief to any group of residents.
A town should adopt whichever tax policy is favored by the majority of its low-income residents.
questions.explanation: The columnist argues that a cheaper rebate would help low-income residents at least as much without the service cuts, so the exemption should be rejected; A captures exactly this reasoning. D is tempting but too broad, and it would also rule out the rebate the columnist favors. B supports the exemption rather than opposing it.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Bramwell should not adopt the grocery sales-tax exemption.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The exemption also cuts taxes for the wealthy; lost revenue would come mostly from library and park budgets that low-income residents rely on; a direct rebate would help low-income residents at least as much at a fraction of the cost.

breakdown.analysis: A principle-justify answer has to tell you to do what the conclusion says: don't adopt the exemption. The premises: there's a cheaper alternative (rebate) that helps the target group at least as much, and the exemption cuts services the group relies on. So we want: if a cheaper option helps the group at least as much without cutting their services, don't adopt the costlier measure. It's like: don't buy your friend a $500 gift card if a $50 one would make them just as happy and you'd have to sell their favorite chair to afford the big one.

choices.note: CORRECT. Measure meant to help a group + cheaper alternative that helps them at least as much + no service cuts → don't adopt. The rebate fits that description, so the exemption should be rejected.
Supports the exemption. If necessities shouldn't be taxed, groceries should be exempt, which is the opposite of the conclusion.
The columnist's reasoning is about who benefits and what services get cut, not only total revenue. "Solely" revenue ignores most of the argument.
Tempting because libraries and parks come up, but it's too broad: it would block any tax relief, including the rebate the columnist recommends. It doesn't capture the cheaper-alternative reasoning.
Majority preference of low-income residents is never mentioned. The argument is about costs and benefits, not polling.

questions.stimulus: Most of the commuters who ride the Linden tram line live in the Harbor district. Most residents of the Harbor district do not own cars. Therefore, most of the commuters who ride the Linden tram line do not own cars.
questions.stem: The flawed pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: Most of the paleontologists at the Ressler Institute study vertebrate fossils. Everyone at the institute who studies vertebrate fossils has done fieldwork abroad. Therefore, most of the paleontologists at the Ressler Institute have done fieldwork abroad.

Most plays staged at the Corbin Theater are comedies, and most comedies staged at the Corbin were written by local playwrights. Therefore, at least some plays staged at the Corbin were written by local playwrights.
Most of the chemists in the Hollis laboratory wear protective gloves while working. Therefore, most of the people in the Hollis laboratory who wear protective gloves while working are chemists.

Most of the documents in the Vell archive were written in Latin. Most documents written in Latin during that era were legal records. Therefore, most of the documents in the Vell archive are legal records.
Most of the plays at the Arden festival were dramas, and most of the plays at the festival sold out. Therefore, most of the dramas at the Arden festival sold out.
questions.explanation: The original chains two 'most' statements (most A are B; most B are C; so most A are C), ignoring that the A's may be among the B's that are not C. D commits the same error. E also combines two 'most' claims, but both describe the same group and the flaw concerns overlap within it, a different structure. A and B are valid, and C reverses a single 'most' statement.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Most Linden tram commuters don't own cars.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Most Linden tram commuters live in the Harbor district; most Harbor district residents don't own cars.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Most A are B; most B are C; so most A are C. (Flawed: the A's may be concentrated among the B's that are not C.)

breakdown.analysis: Chaining "most" through a different middle group doesn't work. Counterexample: Harbor has 10,000 residents, 6,000 carless. The tram has 1,000 riders, 600 from Harbor. Those 600 could all be among the 4,000 car owners. Then most riders own cars. Look for "most A are B; most B are C; so most A are C."

choices.note: Valid. Most paleontologists study vertebrates, and every vertebrate person has done fieldwork, so most paleontologists have done fieldwork. "Everyone" closes the gap that "most" leaves open.
Valid. Most plays are comedies, and most comedies are by locals, so at least some plays are by locals (the comedies by locals are themselves plays). A weak "some" conclusion that does follow.
A different flaw: reversing a single "most." Most chemists wear gloves doesn't mean most glove-wearers are chemists.

CORRECT. Most Vell documents are Latin; most Latin documents were legal records; so most Vell documents are legal records. Most A are B, most B are C, so most A are C. Same gap: the Vell Latin documents could be among the non-legal ones.

Flawed, but differently. Both "most" claims describe the same group (festival plays), and the error is about how much the two majorities overlap. They must overlap somewhat, but not enough for "most dramas." Not the original's chained structure.
